## A note on 2024 IPS data

On 4 September 2026, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) released revised estimates for the International Passenger Survey (IPS)covering the second half of 2024 (Jul-Dec) and in turn 2024 annual estimates. This data is badged as ‘_official statistics in development’_ following the methodological changes introduced in July 2024. They have published these estimates as part of their development work on improving travel and tourism statistics.

The improvements in the estimates released today include the addition of pseudo records (modelled data) for freight travelling to the UK (i.e. lorry drivers via sea and tunnel) which are excluded from the survey collection under the new methodology. The freight pseudo records at Dover are included in the total GB/UK figure and overall business visits but are not included in Europe totals. Freight pseudo records at Eurotunnel are included in the total GB/UK figure, overall business visits and in Europe totals. Neither freight records appear in country totals (so countries accounting for a large number of freight visitors will appear lower than they would under the previous methodology), or nation/region totals. The ONS has also implemented other changes such as their approach to calibration, corrections to destination airport and package holiday spend, so the revision in estimates is a combination of all the above. The ONS has published [an article(opens in a new tab)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/improvingourtravelandtourismstatisticsseptember2026update) outlining these improvements in more detail.

With the improvements to the IPS statistics published on 4 September 2026, VisitBritain notes:

*   The decline in visit numbers in this data is still present for the second half of 2024, compared to 2023, and is in contrast to several other data sources that we have access to, which suggest growth.
*   The addition of freight pseudo records has provided some level of improvement to the estimates. However, there is a still a notable decline in visits via Dover to Calais in the new IPS data, across different vehicle modes, which suggests there is more to explore here.
*   The pseudo records are not available at the market or nations/regions level so data will still be impacted for those visiting from Eastern Europe and some Western European markets, and those visiting Southern and Central England.
*   The ONS is working to improve travel and tourism statistics and so there are some outstanding areas that still need to be investigated. This includes how the new incorporation of NISRA data into the UK estimates is still inconsistent with previous years, and how the new methodology may be impacting some markets more than others.

For transparency and completeness for our users, we have provided data in the pivot tables for total GB on this page and for [nations and regions.](https://www.visitbritain.org/research-insights/inbound-visits-and-spend-annual-regional) We’re working to update the visualisations with new data and have added a note to webpages where we will update data in due course. VisitBritain has included estimates for the second half of 2024 alongside previous time periods in our pivot tables to provide full year numbers for 2024. However, we urge caution when interpreting these estimates and advise users to note the ONS’ badging of the 2024 data as ‘_official statistics in development’._ It is important to note that the ONS themselves do not endorse comparisons with previous years due to the methodology change.

We will continue to work closely with the ONS to understand and address the impact of the methodological changes. In the meantime, users can also explore alternative sources such as the [card spending data](https://www.visitbritain.org/research-insights/card-spending-data). To view a timely update on inbound tourism, please see our [State of the Nation](https://www.visitbritain.org/research-insights/state-nation) report.

## About the survey

The International Passenger Survey (IPS) is a continuous survey carried out by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). It covers all major air, sea and tunnel ports, providing detailed information on the numbers and types of visits made by people travelling to and from the UK.

**Please note due to the ONS’ ongoing planned improvements to the travel and tourism statistics:**

*   2024 final estimates are badged as ‘_official statistics in development’_ and estimates are subject to future change as further improvements to the methods are introduced. The ONS are not endorsing comparisons with previous years.
*   The ONS are also undertaking a review of the historical data, so previous years data may be subject to marginal change.
*   See the latest [update on improvements to the travel and tourism statistics(opens in a new tab)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/improvingourtravelandtourismstatisticsseptember2026update) on the ONS website.

For further information, refer to the[About the IPS](https://www.visitbritain.org/research-insights/about-international-passenger-survey)page.

## A note on 2024 IPS data

On 4 September 2026, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) released revised estimates for the International Passenger Survey (IPS)covering the second half of 2024 (Jul-Dec) and in turn 2024 annual estimates. This data is badged as ‘_official statistics in development’_ following the methodological changes introduced in July 2024. They have published these estimates as part of their development work on improving travel and tourism statistics.

The improvements in the estimates released today include the addition of pseudo records (modelled data) for freight travelling to the UK (i.e. lorry drivers via sea and tunnel) which are excluded from the survey collection under the new methodology. The freight pseudo records at Dover are included in the total GB/UK figure and overall business visits but are not included in Europe totals. Freight pseudo records at Eurotunnel are included in the total GB/UK figure, overall business visits and in Europe totals. Neither freight records appear in country totals (so countries accounting for a large number of freight visitors will appear lower than they would under the previous methodology), or nation/region totals. The ONS has also implemented other changes such as their approach to calibration, corrections to destination airport and package holiday spend, so the revision in estimates is a combination of all the above. The ONS has published [an article(opens in a new tab)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/improvingourtravelandtourismstatisticsseptember2026update) outlining these improvements in more detail.

With the improvements to the IPS statistics published on 4 September 2026, VisitBritain notes:

*   The decline in visit numbers in this data is still present for the second half of 2024, compared to 2023, and is in contrast to several other data sources that we have access to, which suggest growth.
*   The addition of freight pseudo records has provided some level of improvement to the estimates. However, there is a still a notable decline in visits via Dover to Calais in the new IPS data, across different vehicle modes, which suggests there is more to explore here.
*   The pseudo records are not available at the market or nations/regions level so data will still be impacted for those visiting from Eastern Europe and some Western European markets, and those visiting Southern and Central England.
*   The ONS is working to improve travel and tourism statistics and so there are some outstanding areas that still need to be investigated. This includes how the new incorporation of NISRA data into the UK estimates is still inconsistent with previous years, and how the new methodology may be impacting some markets more than others.

For transparency and completeness for our users, we have provided data in the pivot tables for total GB on this page and for [nations and regions.](https://www.visitbritain.org/research-insights/inbound-visits-and-spend-annual-regional) We’re working to update the visualisations with new data and have added a note to webpages where we will update data in due course. VisitBritain has included estimates for the second half of 2024 alongside previous time periods in our pivot tables to provide full year numbers for 2024. However, we urge caution when interpreting these estimates and advise users to note the ONS’ badging of the 2024 data as ‘_official statistics in development’._ It is important to note that the ONS themselves do not endorse comparisons with previous years due to the methodology change.

We will continue to work closely with the ONS to understand and address the impact of the methodological changes. In the meantime, users can also explore alternative sources such as the [card spending data](https://www.visitbritain.org/research-insights/card-spending-data). To view a timely update on inbound tourism, please see our [State of the Nation](https://www.visitbritain.org/research-insights/state-nation) report.

## About the survey

The International Passenger Survey (IPS) is a continuous survey carried out by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). It covers all major air, sea and tunnel ports, providing detailed information on the numbers and types of visits made by people travelling to and from the UK.

**Please note due to the ONS’ ongoing planned improvements to the travel and tourism statistics:**

*   2024 final estimates are badged as ‘_official statistics in development’_ and estimates are subject to future change as further improvements to the methods are introduced. The ONS are not endorsing comparisons with previous years.
*   The ONS are also undertaking a review of the historical data, so previous years data may be subject to marginal change.
*   See the latest [update on improvements to the travel and tourism statistics(opens in a new tab)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/improvingourtravelandtourismstatisticsseptember2026update) on the ONS website.

For further information, refer to the[About the IPS](https://www.visitbritain.org/research-insights/about-international-passenger-survey)page.

# Leisure and tourism

Tourism to the UK, and UK residents travelling abroad, reasons for travel and money spent. The statistics on UK residents travelling abroad are an informal indicator of living standards.

## On this page:

### [Overseas travel and tourism, provisional: January to March and April to June 2025](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/leisureandtourism/bulletins/overseastravelandtourismprovisional/januarytomarchandapriltojune2025)

#### What's in the bulletin?

*   These estimates are published as official statistics in development as we continue to develop and refine our new data collection design and methods implemented in July 2024. This is likely to have led to differences in the estimates compared with those produced using the previous design, the causes of which we are continuing to investigate.
*   Overseas residents made an estimated 7.2 million visits to Great Britain and spent an estimated £4.7 billion in Quarter 1 (Jan to Mar) 2025.
*   Overseas residents made an estimated 9.3 million visits to Great Britain and spent an estimated £7.9 billion in Quarter 2 (Apr to June) 2025.

*   ### [Estimates of visits and spending abroad](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/leisureandtourism/datasets/estimatesofukresidentsvisitsandspendingabroad)

Quarterly estimates of visits and spending abroad. Also includes data on nights, purpose, country visited and mode of travel. The Quarter 4 (Oct to Dec) versions of this dataset up to 2023 are on a different webpage under the name "UK residents visits and expenditure abroad, quarterly". 
*   ### [Estimates of overseas residents’ visits and spending](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/leisureandtourism/datasets/estimatesofoverseasresidentsvisitsandspendingintheuk)

Quarterly estimates of overseas residents’ visits and spending. Also includes data on nights, purpose, region of UK visited and mode of travel. The Quarter 4 (Oct to Dec) versions of this dataset up to 2023 are on a different webpage under the name "Overseas travel and tourism, quarterly". 
*   ### [Travel trends estimates: UK residents' visits abroad](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/leisureandtourism/datasets/ukresidentsvisitsabroad)

We advise against using all editions listed before the 2019 edition. 
*   ### [Travel trends estimates: overseas residents in the UK](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/leisureandtourism/datasets/overseasresidentsvisitstotheuk)

Annual estimates of overseas residents’ visits and spending. Also includes data on nights, purpose, region of UK visited and mode of travel. Breakdowns by nationality and area of residence are covered. In 2019, new methods were introduced for this dataset. The 2009 to 2019 edition supersedes all previous time series editions of this dataset. We advise against using all editions listed before the 2019 edition. 
*   ### [Travelpac: travel to and from the UK](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/leisureandtourism/datasets/travelpac)

Estimates of international visits with details on traveller age and sex, trip purpose, length, and spending. From the International Passenger Survey (IPS).

Tourism: Supporting Key Government
Policies

With the UK poised to leave the European Union this year,
there is a very real need for the Government to support
sectors of the economy that are well positioned to provide
the country with economic growth and create employment
opportunities in the post-Brexit environment.
Tourism is one of the main sectors of the economy that is well placed to achieve
this. The UK continues to be not just one of the most popular destinations in the
world for visitors, but the World Economic Forum continues to rank the UK’s
tourism industry and infrastructure as one of the most competitive in the world.
We are therefore delighted that a Tourism Sector Deal has been agreed under the
Government’s Industrial Strategy. This is only the 10th sector deal to be announced
and highlights the Government’s increasing recognition of the economic importance
of the tourism industry and the opportunities and benefits that it can provide for the
UK economy and in supporting Government policy.
Two very important examples are regional development and soft power.
Regional Development
One of the main challenges for Government is to boost growth outside London and
the South East so as to address both the “North/South” divide and to support the
economies of rural and seaside communities which have lagged behind urban areas
in recovering from the Global Economic Crisis 10 years ago.
Tourism is one of the few industries that can directly support this objective quickly
and without substantial investment in new infrastructure. Despite the growth in city-
breaks, domestic tourism in the UK is largely composed of people in urban areas
travelling to rural and seaside destinations. The £25bn that these visitors spend
on breaks and holidays represents the single largest non-governmental transfer of
wealth to the economies of rural and seaside communities, creating 460,000 fulltime
jobs in these areas.
Soft Power
With the UK leaving the EU, one of the Government’s key objectives is to increase
the UK’s global influence. Tourism is one of the key means of achieving this. Studies
continue to show that enhancing and promoting a country’s cultural and education
offering in overseas markets is a key means of gaining greater global influence.
There strong linkages between the UK’s culture, education and tourism sectors.
Not only is heritage and culture the primary reason that people travel to the UK,
recent research by Universities UK shows that 88% of people who visit the UK for
educational purposes plan to return to the country as tourists  due to the strong
affinity that they build with the country as a result of gaining a qualification.
While the Sector Deal is a significant step forward, it is very much a first step.
There is much more that can be done to boost tourism growth post Brexit. This
publication therefore provides the data to support a range of policies, from tax and
visa reform to resolving structural issues in domestic tourism funding and delivery,
that need to be addressed if we are to maximise tourism growth.

Kate Nicholls
Chair

Tourism: Supporting Key Government
Policies

With the UK poised to leave the European Union this year,
there is a very real need for the Government to support
sectors of the economy that are well positioned to provide
the country with economic growth and create employment
opportunities in the post-Brexit environment.
Tourism is one of the main sectors of the economy that is well placed to achieve
this. The UK continues to be not just one of the most popular destinations in the
world for visitors, but the World Economic Forum continues to rank the UK’s
tourism industry and infrastructure as one of the most competitive in the world.
We are therefore delighted that a Tourism Sector Deal has been agreed under the
Government’s Industrial Strategy. This is only the 10th sector deal to be announced
and highlights the Government’s increasing recognition of the economic importance
of the tourism industry and the opportunities and benefits that it can provide for the
UK economy and in supporting Government policy.
Two very important examples are regional development and soft power.
Regional Development
One of the main challenges for Government is to boost growth outside London and
the South East so as to address both the “North/South” divide and to support the
economies of rural and seaside communities which have lagged behind urban areas
in recovering from the Global Economic Crisis 10 years ago.
Tourism is one of the few industries that can directly support this objective quickly
and without substantial investment in new infrastructure. Despite the growth in city-
breaks, domestic tourism in the UK is largely composed of people in urban areas
travelling to rural and seaside destinations. The £25bn that these visitors spend
on breaks and holidays represents the single largest non-governmental transfer of
wealth to the economies of rural and seaside communities, creating 460,000 fulltime
jobs in these areas.
Soft Power
With the UK leaving the EU, one of the Government’s key objectives is to increase
the UK’s global influence. Tourism is one of the key means of achieving this. Studies
continue to show that enhancing and promoting a country’s cultural and education
offering in overseas markets is a key means of gaining greater global influence.
There strong linkages between the UK’s culture, education and tourism sectors.
Not only is heritage and culture the primary reason that people travel to the UK,
recent research by Universities UK shows that 88% of people who visit the UK for
educational purposes plan to return to the country as tourists  due to the strong
affinity that they build with the country as a result of gaining a qualification.
While the Sector Deal is a significant step forward, it is very much a first step.
There is much more that can be done to boost tourism growth post Brexit. This
publication therefore provides the data to support a range of policies, from tax and
visa reform to resolving structural issues in domestic tourism funding and delivery,
that need to be addressed if we are to maximise tourism growth.

Kate Nicholls
Chair

# Summary 

Inbound and outbound visits to and from the UK were at their highest recorded level in 2024. 2024 was also the first year since the covid-19 pandemic that visitor numbers exceeded 2019 levels. 

The  Office for National Statistics estimated  that tourism directly accounted 

for £58 billion of economic output and supported 1.2 million jobs in 2023. 

This briefing also explains where to find tourism statistics for local areas. 

# Overseas tourism 

In 2024, overseas residents made 42.5 million visits to the UK, compared to 38.0 million visits in 2023. 

The USA, France, Germany and Ireland were the top countries for visitors to Great Britain. Overseas residents spent, in cash terms, £32.5 billion in Great Britain in 2024, compared to £31.1 billion in 2023. 

UK residents made 94.6 million trips overseas in 2024, compared to 86.2 million in 2023. The most popular countries were Spain, France, Italy, Turkey, and the USA. 

# Domestic tourism 

In 2024, British residents made 105.6 million overnight visits within Great Britain, for a total of 308 million nights, and spent £32.9 billion. UK residents made 3.0 million overnight visits within Northern Ireland. 

They also made 1.0 billion tourism day visits, spending £54.8 billion. As such, domestic tourism spending is more valuable than inbound spending. 

Domestic tourism is less focused on London than international tourism. 

# Economic impact 

In 2023,  the ONS estimated  that tourism accounted directly for £58 billion 

(2.4%) of UK economic output. Tourism: Statistics and policy  

> 6Commons Library Research Briefing, 11 February 2026

It estimated that tourism directly accounted for 1.2 million UK jobs in 2023, which was 3.9% of all jobs. 

# Recent issues 

Energy price inflation has  disproportionately affected hospitality businesses 

and the rising cost of living has  reduced consumer demand for travel .

Employment costs have increased, with increases to the  National Minimum 

Wage  and  employer national insurance contributions .

The pound has  lost value against the euro and dollar . This may make the UK a 

more attractive place to holiday for both international and domestic tourists, as the pound is cheaper to buy and more expensive to sell. 

However, the government has ended  VAT-free shopping , removed European 

ID cards  as sufficient ID to enter the UK, and is implementing an  electronic 

travel authorisation  for visitors who do not require a visa. 

# Government policy 

Tourism is a devolved policy area. The government has set an  ambition for 

visitor numbers to the UK to reach 50 million by 2030 , and has said it will 

establish a new  Visitor Economy Advisory Council  to work with industry on 

tourism and design and deliver a new growth strategy. The government  plans 

to publish  a tourism growth strategy later in 2025. Tourism: Statistics and policy

## Minimum wage 

In April 2026, the National Minimum Wage (NMW) will increase by 4.1%, from £12.21 an hour to £12.71 an hour for employees aged 21 and older. This followed a 6.7% increase in April 2025 and a 9.8% increase in April 2024. 38 

According to the Low Pay Commission 2024 report, 21.6% of jobs in the hospitality industry, 17.1% of jobs in the transport industry, and 11.4% of jobs in the leisure industry in 2024 were paid at the minimum wage. This compared to 5.2% of all jobs. 39

The UK has begun requiring that visitors who do not require a visa to visit the UK instead have an electronic travel authorisation (ETA) before they visit. This costs £10 and can be applied for online.

# 6.6 Tax measures 

## Business rates 

Rates relief 

From 2020/21 to 2025/26, the UK government operated a series of temporary business rates relief schemes for properties in the retail, hospitality and leisure (RHL) sectors in England.  49  The Scottish and Welsh governments operated their own relief schemes. 

RHL relief has not been extended beyond 2025/26 in England, although there in January 2026 the government announced an additional 15% relief for 2026/27 for pubs and live music venues. Instead, the UK government is introducing a permanently lower multiplier for RHL businesses. 

Rates reform 

The government has set two new multipliers which will apply to RHL businesses from 2026/27 until 2028/29. For RHL businesses with a rateable value below £51,000, the multiplier is five pence below the small business multiplier. For RHL businesses with a rateable value above £51,000, but below £500,000, the multiplier is five pence below the standard multiplier. The two non-RHL multipliers are ordinarily uprated with inflation. There is further information about RHL business rates in Section 3 of the Library briefing  Business rates: the 2026 revaluation .

## VAT 

The standard rate of VAT has been 20% since January 2011. VAT was temporarily reduced (initially to 5%, and then to 12.5%) between July 2020 and March 2022. 50 

There has been a long-running campaign by the tourism and hospitality sector for a lower rate of VAT to be set on services supplied to tourists. The Library briefing  VAT on tourism and hospitality services  has further 

information.

## Tax-free shopping 

As a member of the EU, the UK was required to have a tax-free shopping scheme. This allowed non-EU residents to claim back the VAT on goods purchased in the UK and taken home by the visitor. 51 

At the end of the Brexit transition period on 31 December 2020, the government withdrew the scheme in Great Britain, though it remains in Northern Ireland. 

The Office for Budget Responsibility estimated (subject to significant uncertainty) in March 2024 that ending tax-free shopping would increase tax revenue by around £2 billion from 2020/21 to 2025/26. 52 

The Library briefing  Tax-free shopping for international visitors  discusses the 

arguments for and against tax-free shopping. The government has “no plans” to reintroduce tax-free shopping.  53 

## Furnished holiday lets (FHLs) 

Prior to April 2025, landlords renting out property that qualified as a ‘furnished holiday letting’ were entitled to certain tax benefits, compared with landlords renting out other types of residential property. 54  Since the FHL tax regime was abolished, landlords letting FHLs have only had access to the same reliefs available to other types of landlords and property businesses. 

## Tourist taxes 

The government is consulting on allowing mayoral authorities in England to introduce an overnight visitor levy. The Scottish and Welsh parliaments have both passed legislation allowing local authorities to introduce a visitor levy.  55 

The Library briefing  Visitor levies: policy and debates  has more information.

# Summary 

Inbound and outbound visits to and from the UK were at their highest recorded level in 2024. 2024 was also the first year since the covid-19 pandemic that visitor numbers exceeded 2019 levels. 

The  Office for National Statistics estimated  that tourism directly accounted 

for £58 billion of economic output and supported 1.2 million jobs in 2023. 

This briefing also explains where to find tourism statistics for local areas. 

# Overseas tourism 

In 2024, overseas residents made 42.5 million visits to the UK, compared to 38.0 million visits in 2023. 

The USA, France, Germany and Ireland were the top countries for visitors to Great Britain. Overseas residents spent, in cash terms, £32.5 billion in Great Britain in 2024, compared to £31.1 billion in 2023. 

UK residents made 94.6 million trips overseas in 2024, compared to 86.2 million in 2023. The most popular countries were Spain, France, Italy, Turkey, and the USA. 

# Domestic tourism 

In 2024, British residents made 105.6 million overnight visits within Great Britain, for a total of 308 million nights, and spent £32.9 billion. UK residents made 3.0 million overnight visits within Northern Ireland. 

They also made 1.0 billion tourism day visits, spending £54.8 billion. As such, domestic tourism spending is more valuable than inbound spending. 

Domestic tourism is less focused on London than international tourism. 

# Economic impact 

In 2023,  the ONS estimated  that tourism accounted directly for £58 billion 

(2.4%) of UK economic output. Tourism: Statistics and policy  

> 6Commons Library Research Briefing, 11 February 2026

It estimated that tourism directly accounted for 1.2 million UK jobs in 2023, which was 3.9% of all jobs. 

# Recent issues 

Energy price inflation has  disproportionately affected hospitality businesses 

and the rising cost of living has  reduced consumer demand for travel .

Employment costs have increased, with increases to the  National Minimum 

Wage  and  employer national insurance contributions .

The pound has  lost value against the euro and dollar . This may make the UK a 

more attractive place to holiday for both international and domestic tourists, as the pound is cheaper to buy and more expensive to sell. 

However, the government has ended  VAT-free shopping , removed European 

ID cards  as sufficient ID to enter the UK, and is implementing an  electronic 

travel authorisation  for visitors who do not require a visa. 

# Government policy 

Tourism is a devolved policy area. The government has set an  ambition for 

visitor numbers to the UK to reach 50 million by 2030 , and has said it will 

establish a new  Visitor Economy Advisory Council  to work with industry on 

tourism and design and deliver a new growth strategy. The government  plans 

to publish  a tourism growth strategy later in 2025. Tourism: Statistics and policy

## 1 Data collection and definitions 

Data on visitor numbers is collected using the International 

Passenger Survey, which surveys travellers at major air, sea and 

tunnel ports. 

A visit is a trip made by an overseas resident (someone who 

resides permanently outside of the UK) for a period of less than 12 

months. Some day visits will be included in the total, but day 

visits between Ireland and Northern Ireland are not counted. 2

As of April 2024, the ONS no longer collect International 

Passenger Survey data in Northern Ireland; data on tourism in 

Northern Ireland is now collected by the  Northern Ireland 

Statistics and Research Agency . This means that headline figures 

for 2024 include Northern Ireland, but the detailed figures (for 

example, on visitor origins or spending) are for Great Britain. 3

## Length of visits 

Overseas visitors spent around 288 million nights in Great Britain in 2024, down on 293 million in 2023. The average length of visit was 7.4 nights in 2024, compared to 7.7 in 2023; visitors took more but shorter trips in 2024 compared to 2023. 6

# 3 Domestic tourism 

# 3.1 Overnight visits 

In 2024, residents of Great Britain made 105.6 million overnight visits within Great Britain, which is a 10% decrease on the number of visits in 2023. 

Domestic overnight tourists spent a total of £32.9 billion in 2024. This is slightly greater than spending by international tourists in the same year (£32.5 billion). 

38% of trips were to visit friends and family, 30% for holidays, 27% for miscellaneous reasons, and 6% for business. 14 

## Destinations 

In 2024, there were 99 million trips made to England, 11 million to Scotland, and 8 million to Wales by residents of Great Britain. 15 

England 

Domestic overnight visits to England are more spread out throughout the country than international visits. Of the 90 million visits to England, 15 million each (17%) were to London and the South West, and 14 million each (16%) to the North West and the South East. 

London accounted for the most spending (£5.4 billion or 20%), followed by the South West (£4.5 billion or 17%) and the North West (£4.3 billion or 16%). 16 

Scotland 

37% of trips to Scotland were to the West of Scotland (including Glasgow), 36% were to the East of Scotland (including Edinburgh), 25% to the North of Scotland, and 7% to the South of Scotland. 

57% of overnight trips in Scotland were by people resident in Scotland. 42% of visitors were from England and 2% from Wales.  17

In 2024, residents of Great Britain made 1.0 billion tourism day visits and spent £54.8 billion, a decrease of 12% from 2023.

## 2 Data collection and definitions 

Data on domestic tourism is collected using the Great Britain 

Tourism Survey. 

A domestic overnight trip is a trip involving a stay of at least one 

night that is not taken on a frequent basis. A domestic day trip is a 

leisure trip of at least three hours. A domestic tourism day trip is 

an irregular leisure trip, usually to a different local authority. 

The definition of both overnight and day visits was changed in 

2021, and therefore data from before and after the pandemic 

cannot be directly compared. 20 Tourism: Statistics and policy

# 4 Finding local tourism statistics 

Statistics on tourism visits and tourism spending are not available by constituency, but some data is available at county level. 

This section sets out the main official sources for tourism statistics for local areas. In addition to the sources set out here, local authorities and tourism bodies (see section 7.3) may also produce or commission their own statistics and reports. 

# Domestic visitors 

VisitBritain publishes  information about the number of domestic day and 

overnight trips by county . Data is published as a two-year rolling average, 

with the most recent data for 2024.  22 

# International visitors 

The ONS publishes  data from the International Passenger Survey by county  on 

an annual basis (see the single-year annual spreadsheets). 23  The most recent release is from 2024, and includes data on purpose of visit, nights stayed, and spending. 

The International Passenger Survey data also includes data on international visits to the top 50 UK cities and towns by number of visitors. Data is available about visitors’ country of residence, age, purpose of visit, nights stayed, and spending. 

VisitBritain publishes the  number of international visitors to towns, cities, and 

national parks , also based on the International Passenger Survey. The most 

recent data is from 2023. However, particularly for smaller towns, visitor numbers may be very small and should be treated as rough estimates. 24

# 6 Issues affecting the sector 

According to the Business Insights and Conditions Survey, conducted by the Office for National Statistics (ONS), the costs of materials and labour were the main challenges impacting food and accommodation businesses’ turnover in November 2025. 31 

# 6.1 Inflation 

At its peak in October 2022, annual inflation (measured by the Consumer Price Index) was 11.1%. Inflation on food and non-alcoholic beverages peaked at 19.2% in March 2023. As of December 2025, annual inflation was 3.4%, and inflation on food and non-alcoholic beverages was 4.5%. 32 

## Energy prices 

The average electricity unit price for UK non-domestic users increased 92% between 2021 and 2023. The average unit price has fallen since, but remained 75% higher in Q4 2024 when compared to Q1 2021. Average gas unit prices also more than doubled between 2021 and 2024.  33 

In March 2025, UK Hospitality called for the Competition and Markets Authority to investigate the “entrenched competition problems” in the non-domestic energy market. 34 

Going into August 2025, energy prices were still a significant concern for hospitality businesses; 16% said it was the main concern for their business, compared to 5% of all businesses. 35

## Effects on visitors 

In August 2024, the Resolution Foundation estimated that real non-pensioner median incomes fell by 3% between 2019/20 and 2023/24. 36 

According to Visit England’s January 2026 Domestic Sentiment Tracker, which surveys UK residents to monitor barriers to travel, 60% of people reported either being “very careful” or “cutting back” in response to the cost-of-living crisis. 30% of respondents mentioned the “rising cost of living” as a barrier to taking a domestic trip in the UK within the next six months, the same proportion as mentioned the weather. 37 

# 6.2 Staffing 

## Minimum wage 

In April 2026, the National Minimum Wage (NMW) will increase by 4.1%, from £12.21 an hour to £12.71 an hour for employees aged 21 and older. This followed a 6.7% increase in April 2025 and a 9.8% increase in April 2024. 38 

According to the Low Pay Commission 2024 report, 21.6% of jobs in the hospitality industry, 17.1% of jobs in the transport industry, and 11.4% of jobs in the leisure industry in 2024 were paid at the minimum wage. This compared to 5.2% of all jobs. 39 

There is more information on the National Minimum Wage in the Library research briefing  National Minimum Wage statistics .

## Employer NICs 

In the Autumn Budget 2024, the Chancellor increased the rate of employer National Insurance contributions (NICs) from 13.8% to 15.0%. These changes came into effect in April 2025. 

The Secondary Threshold (the earnings threshold over which employers must pay NICs) was reduced from £9,100 a year to £5,000 a year. 40 

The Employment Allowance (which reduces an employer’s total NICs liability) was increased from £5,000 to £10,500.

# 6.3 Electronic travel authorisations (ETAs) 

The UK has begun requiring that visitors who do not require a visa to visit the UK instead have an electronic travel authorisation (ETA) before they visit. This costs £10 and can be applied for online. 

Since April 2025, an ETA has been required for all non-visa nationals (people who do not usually need a visa to visit the UK). 42  Prior to the rollout of the ETA, people from various countries, including EU and US nationals, did not require any advance permission before travelling. Now, only Irish residents are able to visit the UK without any form of advance permission. 

The ETA has been raised as a particular issue for UK tourism with respect to tourism across the land border in Ireland. 43  Non-visa nationals visiting Ireland, prior to the ETA, could add on a trip into Northern Ireland with no UK immigration implications. They will now be expected to have an ETA or risk committing a criminal offence. This is particularly pertinent for coach and group tours.  44 

# 6.4 Value of the pound 

Over the last ten years, the pound has been relatively weak against the dollar, as shown in the graph below. The Library briefing on  Sterling exchange 

rates  has the latest data. 

A weaker pound means that it is generally cheaper for overseas residents to visit the UK, which makes the UK relatively more attractive. It also makes staying in the UK relatively more attractive to UK tourists compared to travelling abroad. 45

# 6.5 EU visitor passport requirements 

Prior to October 2021, EU nationals were able to enter the UK using their EU ID card. However, they now need to have a passport. 46 

This is a barrier to travel for EU residents who don’t own a passport, and has been raised as a particular barrier for school children and young people.  47 

The UK has an agreement with France that permits French schoolchildren travelling on organised trips to travel using national identity cards and waives UK visa requirements for their classmates who are visa nationals (who usually would require a visa to visit the UK). Children travelling as part of a French school trip will also be temporarily exempt from ETA requirements. 48 

As of February 2026, this arrangement has not been extended to other EU countries.

# 6.6 Tax measures 

## Business rates 

Rates relief 

From 2020/21 to 2025/26, the UK government operated a series of temporary business rates relief schemes for properties in the retail, hospitality and leisure (RHL) sectors in England.  49  The Scottish and Welsh governments operated their own relief schemes. 

RHL relief has not been extended beyond 2025/26 in England, although there in January 2026 the government announced an additional 15% relief for 2026/27 for pubs and live music venues. Instead, the UK government is introducing a permanently lower multiplier for RHL businesses. 

Rates reform 

The government has set two new multipliers which will apply to RHL businesses from 2026/27 until 2028/29. For RHL businesses with a rateable value below £51,000, the multiplier is five pence below the small business multiplier. For RHL businesses with a rateable value above £51,000, but below £500,000, the multiplier is five pence below the standard multiplier. The two non-RHL multipliers are ordinarily uprated with inflation. There is further information about RHL business rates in Section 3 of the Library briefing  Business rates: the 2026 revaluation .

## VAT 

The standard rate of VAT has been 20% since January 2011. VAT was temporarily reduced (initially to 5%, and then to 12.5%) between July 2020 and March 2022. 50 

There has been a long-running campaign by the tourism and hospitality sector for a lower rate of VAT to be set on services supplied to tourists. The Library briefing  VAT on tourism and hospitality services  has further 

information.

## Tax-free shopping 

As a member of the EU, the UK was required to have a tax-free shopping scheme. This allowed non-EU residents to claim back the VAT on goods purchased in the UK and taken home by the visitor. 51 

At the end of the Brexit transition period on 31 December 2020, the government withdrew the scheme in Great Britain, though it remains in Northern Ireland. 

The Office for Budget Responsibility estimated (subject to significant uncertainty) in March 2024 that ending tax-free shopping would increase tax revenue by around £2 billion from 2020/21 to 2025/26. 52 

The Library briefing  Tax-free shopping for international visitors  discusses the 

arguments for and against tax-free shopping. The government has “no plans” to reintroduce tax-free shopping.  53 

## Furnished holiday lets (FHLs) 

Prior to April 2025, landlords renting out property that qualified as a ‘furnished holiday letting’ were entitled to certain tax benefits, compared with landlords renting out other types of residential property. 54  Since the FHL tax regime was abolished, landlords letting FHLs have only had access to the same reliefs available to other types of landlords and property businesses. 

## Tourist taxes 

The government is consulting on allowing mayoral authorities in England to introduce an overnight visitor levy. The Scottish and Welsh parliaments have both passed legislation allowing local authorities to introduce a visitor levy.  55 

The Library briefing  Visitor levies: policy and debates  has more information.

Cite this workReuse this work

*   Introduction
*   Charts

Tourism has massively increased in recent decades. Aviation has opened up travel from domestic to international. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of international visits had more than doubled since 2000.

Tourism can be important for both the travelers and the people in the countries they visit.

For visitors, traveling can increase their understanding of and appreciation for people in other countries and their cultures.

And in many countries, many people rely on tourism for their income. In some, it is one of the largest industries.

But tourism also has externalities: it [contributes](https://ourworldindata.org/co2-emissions-from-aviation) to global carbon emissions and can encroach on local environments and cultures.

On this page, you can find data and visualizations on the history and current state of tourism across the world.

# Tourism

By [Bastian Herre](https://ourworldindata.org/team/bastian-herre) and [Veronika Samborska](https://ourworldindata.org/team/veronika-samborska)

Cite this workReuse this work

*   Introduction
*   Charts

Tourism has massively increased in recent decades. Aviation has opened up travel from domestic to international. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of international visits had more than doubled since 2000.

Tourism can be important for both the travelers and the people in the countries they visit.

For visitors, traveling can increase their understanding of and appreciation for people in other countries and their cultures.

And in many countries, many people rely on tourism for their income. In some, it is one of the largest industries.

But tourism also has externalities: it [contributes](https://ourworldindata.org/co2-emissions-from-aviation) to global carbon emissions and can encroach on local environments and cultures.

On this page, you can find data and visualizations on the history and current state of tourism across the world.

|Definition|Overview (Dec 1, 2025)

 In the latest reporting year for each country (2024 for some countries, and 2023 or 2022 for others depending on data availability from UNWTO), a clear recovery of international tourist flows after the pandemic can be observed, albeit with pronounced differentiation across regions and major markets. Europe shows the strongest recovery dynamics: Spain demonstrates sustained growth, with 137.64 million international arrivals in 2024 compared with 107.14 million in 2014, implying an increase of roughly 30 million tourists over ten years and a clear outperformance relative to most competitors. Italy and the United Kingdom also remain major tourism magnets: Italy has recorded growth in recent years and reaches more than 88 million arrivals in 2024, while the United Kingdom has returned to levels of around 39 million in 2024. European leaders recovered the fastest, supported by reopened air connectivity and strong demand for beach and cultural destinations.  
  
 Asia presents a mixed picture. Japan has grown significantly, reaching approximately 36.87 million arrivals in 2024 compared with about 13.4 million in 2014, indicating a multiple-fold increase over ten years and a strong post-pandemic tourism rebound. South Korea also recorded a substantial recovery to around 16.4 million arrivals in 2024. By contrast, China shows an opposite trend: the latest available data remain well below pre-pandemic peaks, with inbound tourism falling from several tens of millions in the pre-crisis years to approximately 25.25 million in the most recent period, reflecting the impact of prolonged restrictions and a slower recovery of inbound travel.  
  
 In North and Latin America, Mexico and the Dominican Republic are the leading performers. Mexico shows further strengthening in 2024, with more than 86.4 million arrivals, exceeding its 2014–2016 levels. The United States, in the most recent available years, has recovered close to pre-crisis volumes (roughly 171–175 million arrivals before and after the pandemic), confirming the resilience of domestic and inbound demand for U.S. destinations. The Dominican Republic has also returned to high levels, exceeding 11 million arrivals in 2024 and remaining a key Caribbean tourism hub.  
  
 In Africa and the Middle East, trends are divergent. South Africa shows steady long-term growth and reached approximately 11.4 million arrivals in 2024, while several African markets remain well below their potential. Saudi Arabia has recorded a sharp increase in tourist arrivals in recent years and in 2024 reached multi-million levels (around 33.5 million), reflecting targeted investments in the tourism industry and new visa and tourism product initiatives.  
  
 Over longer horizons (10–20 years), the main growth leaders include Spain, Italy, Japan, and several Caribbean and Mediterranean economies, which have added tens of millions of arrivals compared with the 2004–2014 period. China stands out as a relative underperformer over the period due to the sharp decline in inbound tourism after its pre-pandemic peak; similarly, several countries experienced deep declines in 2020–2021, with recovery taking longer. Compared with the beginning of the period (mid-1990s), many European markets have doubled or multiplied their tourist flows several times, while some Asian markets have shown more volatile dynamics due to policy-specific factors and restrictions.  
  
**The underlying drivers of these trends** include a combination of structural growth in air connectivity and tourism infrastructure in some countries, active government support for tourism and marketing (including the opening of new resorts and liberal visa regimes), and, at the same time, epidemiological restrictions, changes in visa policy, and geopolitical factors in others. Large markets that invested in tourism products and eased entry requirements have already benefited from faster recovery.  
  
**Statbase outlook**: over the next two to three years, further strengthening of international tourist flows is expected in Europe and in countries actively developing tourism products and liberalizing visa regimes. Japan and several Asian destinations are likely to continue growing, provided air travel accessibility remains favorable. China, with the normalization of domestic and international rules, could demonstrate a rapid rebound toward previous scales, which would alter the regional balance; however, this outcome depends on the stabilization of political and sanitary conditions. Risks remain associated with new epidemic waves, geopolitical shocks, and air transport price dynamics, which could restrain recovery in certain markets.

|Definition|Overview (Dec 1, 2025)

 In the latest reporting year for each country (2024 for some countries, and 2023 or 2022 for others depending on data availability from UNWTO), a clear recovery of international tourist flows after the pandemic can be observed, albeit with pronounced differentiation across regions and major markets. Europe shows the strongest recovery dynamics: Spain demonstrates sustained growth, with 137.64 million international arrivals in 2024 compared with 107.14 million in 2014, implying an increase of roughly 30 million tourists over ten years and a clear outperformance relative to most competitors. Italy and the United Kingdom also remain major tourism magnets: Italy has recorded growth in recent years and reaches more than 88 million arrivals in 2024, while the United Kingdom has returned to levels of around 39 million in 2024. European leaders recovered the fastest, supported by reopened air connectivity and strong demand for beach and cultural destinations.  
  
 Asia presents a mixed picture. Japan has grown significantly, reaching approximately 36.87 million arrivals in 2024 compared with about 13.4 million in 2014, indicating a multiple-fold increase over ten years and a strong post-pandemic tourism rebound. South Korea also recorded a substantial recovery to around 16.4 million arrivals in 2024. By contrast, China shows an opposite trend: the latest available data remain well below pre-pandemic peaks, with inbound tourism falling from several tens of millions in the pre-crisis years to approximately 25.25 million in the most recent period, reflecting the impact of prolonged restrictions and a slower recovery of inbound travel.  
  
 In North and Latin America, Mexico and the Dominican Republic are the leading performers. Mexico shows further strengthening in 2024, with more than 86.4 million arrivals, exceeding its 2014–2016 levels. The United States, in the most recent available years, has recovered close to pre-crisis volumes (roughly 171–175 million arrivals before and after the pandemic), confirming the resilience of domestic and inbound demand for U.S. destinations. The Dominican Republic has also returned to high levels, exceeding 11 million arrivals in 2024 and remaining a key Caribbean tourism hub.  
  
 In Africa and the Middle East, trends are divergent. South Africa shows steady long-term growth and reached approximately 11.4 million arrivals in 2024, while several African markets remain well below their potential. Saudi Arabia has recorded a sharp increase in tourist arrivals in recent years and in 2024 reached multi-million levels (around 33.5 million), reflecting targeted investments in the tourism industry and new visa and tourism product initiatives.  
  
 Over longer horizons (10–20 years), the main growth leaders include Spain, Italy, Japan, and several Caribbean and Mediterranean economies, which have added tens of millions of arrivals compared with the 2004–2014 period. China stands out as a relative underperformer over the period due to the sharp decline in inbound tourism after its pre-pandemic peak; similarly, several countries experienced deep declines in 2020–2021, with recovery taking longer. Compared with the beginning of the period (mid-1990s), many European markets have doubled or multiplied their tourist flows several times, while some Asian markets have shown more volatile dynamics due to policy-specific factors and restrictions.  
  
**The underlying drivers of these trends** include a combination of structural growth in air connectivity and tourism infrastructure in some countries, active government support for tourism and marketing (including the opening of new resorts and liberal visa regimes), and, at the same time, epidemiological restrictions, changes in visa policy, and geopolitical factors in others. Large markets that invested in tourism products and eased entry requirements have already benefited from faster recovery.  
  
**Statbase outlook**: over the next two to three years, further strengthening of international tourist flows is expected in Europe and in countries actively developing tourism products and liberalizing visa regimes. Japan and several Asian destinations are likely to continue growing, provided air travel accessibility remains favorable. China, with the normalization of domestic and international rules, could demonstrate a rapid rebound toward previous scales, which would alter the regional balance; however, this outcome depends on the stabilization of political and sanitary conditions. Risks remain associated with new epidemic waves, geopolitical shocks, and air transport price dynamics, which could restrain recovery in certain markets.

## A note on 2024 IPS data

On 4 September 2026, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) released revised estimates for the International Passenger Survey (IPS)covering the second half of 2024 (Jul-Dec) and in turn 2024 annual estimates. This data is badged as ‘_official statistics in development’_ following the methodological changes introduced in July 2024. They have published these estimates as part of their development work on improving travel and tourism statistics.

The improvements in the estimates released today include the addition of pseudo records (modelled data) for freight travelling to the UK (i.e. lorry drivers via sea and tunnel) which are excluded from the survey collection under the new methodology. The freight pseudo records at Dover are included in the total GB/UK figure and overall business visits but are not included in Europe totals. Freight pseudo records at Eurotunnel are included in the total GB/UK figure, overall business visits and in Europe totals. Neither freight records appear in country totals (so countries accounting for a large number of freight visitors will appear lower than they would under the previous methodology), or nation/region totals. The ONS has also implemented other changes such as their approach to calibration, corrections to destination airport and package holiday spend, so the revision in estimates is a combination of all the above. The ONS has published [an article(opens in a new tab)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/improvingourtravelandtourismstatisticsseptember2026update) outlining these improvements in more detail.

With the improvements to the IPS statistics published on 4 September 2026, VisitBritain notes:

*   The decline in visit numbers in this data is still present for the second half of 2024, compared to 2023, and is in contrast to several other data sources that we have access to, which suggest growth.

*   The addition of freight pseudo records has provided some level of improvement to the estimates. However, there is a still a notable decline in visits via Dover to Calais in the new IPS data, across different vehicle modes, which suggests there is more to explore here.

*   The pseudo records are not available at the market or nations/regions level so data will still be impacted for those visiting from Eastern Europe and some Western European markets, and those visiting Southern and Central England.

*   The ONS is working to improve travel and tourism statistics and so there are some outstanding areas that still need to be investigated. This includes how the new incorporation of NISRA data into the UK estimates is still inconsistent with previous years, and how the new methodology may be impacting some markets more than others.

For transparency and completeness for our users, we have provided data in the pivot tables for total GB and for nations and regions on this page. We’re working to update the visualisations with new data and have added a note to webpages where we will update data in due course.VisitBritain has included estimates for the second half of 2024 alongside previous time periods in our pivot tables to provide full year numbers for 2024. However, we urge caution when interpreting these estimates and advise users to note the ONS’ badging of the 2024 data as ‘_official statistics in development’._ It is important to note that the ONS themselves do not endorse comparisons with previous years due to the methodology change.

We will continue to work closely with the ONS to understand and address the impact of the methodological changes. In the meantime, users can also explore alternative sources such as the [card spending data](https://www.visitbritain.org/research-insights/card-spending-data). To view a timely update on inbound tourism, please see our [State of the Nation](https://www.visitbritain.org/research-insights/state-nation) report.

## About the survey

The International Passenger Survey (IPS) is a continuous survey carried out by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). It covers all major air, sea and tunnel ports, providing detailed information on the numbers and types of visits made by people travelling to and from the UK.

**Please note due to the ONS’ ongoing planned improvements to the travel and tourism statistics:**

*   2024 final estimates are badged as ‘_official statistics in development’_ and estimates are subject to future change as further improvements to the methods are introduced. The ONS are not endorsing comparisons with previous years.

*   The ONS are also undertaking a review of the historical data, so previous years data may be subject to marginal change.

*   See the latest [update on improvements to the travel and tourism statistics(opens in a new tab)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/improvingourtravelandtourismstatisticsseptember2026update) on the ONS website.

For further information, refer to the[About the IPS](https://www.visitbritain.org/research-insights/about-international-passenger-survey)page.

*   ### Interpreting regional data

**An important note about the survey’s methodology when interpreting regional data:**

    *   Visitors who spend at least one night in the UK during their trip are asked where they stayed. This information can be aggregated to look at the number of visits, nights, and spending in different regions, cities, and towns.
    *   Information at the regional level is often based on very small sample sizes, and as such should be treated with extreme caution, and used solely as an indicative estimate. The IPS is a national survey, and is not designed to be statistically robust at the regional level.
    *   Visitors often spend nights in more than one location during their trip. This means that ‘visits’ values for different regions will not sum to the national total – for example a visitor from the US making a single visit to the UK could be counted as making a ‘staying visit’ to London, to Edinburgh and to Chester.
    *   The data includes a ‘Total UK’ category, representing the true national total for visits.
    *   ‘Double counting’ is not an issue when looking at visitor nights or spending.
    *   No information is recorded about where visitors arriving or departing the UK on the same day travel during their trip, nor is information recorded about where ‘staying visitors’ go for ‘day trips’. If a visitor from France spends four nights in Edinburgh, they may take a day trip to St Andrews and another to Stirling, but this information will not be recorded in the IPS.

**A note on the English regions**

Data for each of the English regions can be viewed individually, or at an aggregated level. The aggregated levels available are:

    *   Rest of England: all regions outside London combined.
    *   England’s North Country: North East, North West and Yorkshire combined.
    *   Central England: West Midlands, East Midlands and East of England combined.
    *   Southern England: South East and South West combined.

## Data warning

2024 ESTIMATES ARE ‘OFFICIAL STATISTICS IN DEVELOPMENT’. THE ONS ARE NOT ENDORSING COMPARISONS WITH PREVIOUS YEARS. SEE THE [ONS WEBSITE(opens in a new tab)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/improvingourtravelandtourismstatisticsseptember2026update) FOR MORE INFORMATION.

## A note on 2024 IPS data

On 4 September 2026, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) released revised estimates for the International Passenger Survey (IPS)covering the second half of 2024 (Jul-Dec) and in turn 2024 annual estimates. This data is badged as ‘_official statistics in development’_ following the methodological changes introduced in July 2024. They have published these estimates as part of their development work on improving travel and tourism statistics.

The improvements in the estimates released today include the addition of pseudo records (modelled data) for freight travelling to the UK (i.e. lorry drivers via sea and tunnel) which are excluded from the survey collection under the new methodology. The freight pseudo records at Dover are included in the total GB/UK figure and overall business visits but are not included in Europe totals. Freight pseudo records at Eurotunnel are included in the total GB/UK figure, overall business visits and in Europe totals. Neither freight records appear in country totals (so countries accounting for a large number of freight visitors will appear lower than they would under the previous methodology), or nation/region totals. The ONS has also implemented other changes such as their approach to calibration, corrections to destination airport and package holiday spend, so the revision in estimates is a combination of all the above. The ONS has published [an article(opens in a new tab)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/improvingourtravelandtourismstatisticsseptember2026update) outlining these improvements in more detail.

With the improvements to the IPS statistics published on 4 September 2026, VisitBritain notes:

*   The decline in visit numbers in this data is still present for the second half of 2024, compared to 2023, and is in contrast to several other data sources that we have access to, which suggest growth.

*   The addition of freight pseudo records has provided some level of improvement to the estimates. However, there is a still a notable decline in visits via Dover to Calais in the new IPS data, across different vehicle modes, which suggests there is more to explore here.

*   The pseudo records are not available at the market or nations/regions level so data will still be impacted for those visiting from Eastern Europe and some Western European markets, and those visiting Southern and Central England.

*   The ONS is working to improve travel and tourism statistics and so there are some outstanding areas that still need to be investigated. This includes how the new incorporation of NISRA data into the UK estimates is still inconsistent with previous years, and how the new methodology may be impacting some markets more than others.

For transparency and completeness for our users, we have provided data in the pivot tables for total GB and for nations and regions on this page. We’re working to update the visualisations with new data and have added a note to webpages where we will update data in due course.VisitBritain has included estimates for the second half of 2024 alongside previous time periods in our pivot tables to provide full year numbers for 2024. However, we urge caution when interpreting these estimates and advise users to note the ONS’ badging of the 2024 data as ‘_official statistics in development’._ It is important to note that the ONS themselves do not endorse comparisons with previous years due to the methodology change.

We will continue to work closely with the ONS to understand and address the impact of the methodological changes. In the meantime, users can also explore alternative sources such as the [card spending data](https://www.visitbritain.org/research-insights/card-spending-data). To view a timely update on inbound tourism, please see our [State of the Nation](https://www.visitbritain.org/research-insights/state-nation) report.

## About the survey

The International Passenger Survey (IPS) is a continuous survey carried out by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). It covers all major air, sea and tunnel ports, providing detailed information on the numbers and types of visits made by people travelling to and from the UK.

**Please note due to the ONS’ ongoing planned improvements to the travel and tourism statistics:**

*   2024 final estimates are badged as ‘_official statistics in development’_ and estimates are subject to future change as further improvements to the methods are introduced. The ONS are not endorsing comparisons with previous years.

*   The ONS are also undertaking a review of the historical data, so previous years data may be subject to marginal change.

*   See the latest [update on improvements to the travel and tourism statistics(opens in a new tab)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/improvingourtravelandtourismstatisticsseptember2026update) on the ONS website.

For further information, refer to the[About the IPS](https://www.visitbritain.org/research-insights/about-international-passenger-survey)page.

*   ### Interpreting regional data

**An important note about the survey’s methodology when interpreting regional data:**

    *   Visitors who spend at least one night in the UK during their trip are asked where they stayed. This information can be aggregated to look at the number of visits, nights, and spending in different regions, cities, and towns.
    *   Information at the regional level is often based on very small sample sizes, and as such should be treated with extreme caution, and used solely as an indicative estimate. The IPS is a national survey, and is not designed to be statistically robust at the regional level.
    *   Visitors often spend nights in more than one location during their trip. This means that ‘visits’ values for different regions will not sum to the national total – for example a visitor from the US making a single visit to the UK could be counted as making a ‘staying visit’ to London, to Edinburgh and to Chester.
    *   The data includes a ‘Total UK’ category, representing the true national total for visits.
    *   ‘Double counting’ is not an issue when looking at visitor nights or spending.
    *   No information is recorded about where visitors arriving or departing the UK on the same day travel during their trip, nor is information recorded about where ‘staying visitors’ go for ‘day trips’. If a visitor from France spends four nights in Edinburgh, they may take a day trip to St Andrews and another to Stirling, but this information will not be recorded in the IPS.

**A note on the English regions**

Data for each of the English regions can be viewed individually, or at an aggregated level. The aggregated levels available are:

    *   Rest of England: all regions outside London combined.
    *   England’s North Country: North East, North West and Yorkshire combined.
    *   Central England: West Midlands, East Midlands and East of England combined.
    *   Southern England: South East and South West combined.

Tourism to the UK, and UK residents travelling abroad, reasons for travel and money spent. The statistics on UK residents travelling abroad are an informal indicator of living standards.

# Leisure and tourism

Tourism to the UK, and UK residents travelling abroad, reasons for travel and money spent. The statistics on UK residents travelling abroad are an informal indicator of living standards.

## On this page:

#### What's in the bulletin?

*   These estimates are published as official statistics in development as we continue to develop and refine our new data collection design and methods implemented in July 2024. This is likely to have led to differences in the estimates compared with those produced using the previous design, the causes of which we are continuing to investigate.
*   Overseas residents made an estimated 7.2 million visits to Great Britain and spent an estimated £4.7 billion in Quarter 1 (Jan to Mar) 2025.

## Datasets related to Leisure and tourism

*   ### [Estimates of visits and spending abroad](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/leisureandtourism/datasets/estimatesofukresidentsvisitsandspendingabroad)

Quarterly estimates of visits and spending abroad. Also includes data on nights, purpose, country visited and mode of travel. The Quarter 4 (Oct to Dec) versions of this dataset up to 2023 are on a different webpage under the name "UK residents visits and expenditure abroad, quarterly". 
*   ### [Estimates of overseas residents’ visits and spending](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/leisureandtourism/datasets/estimatesofoverseasresidentsvisitsandspendingintheuk)

Quarterly estimates of overseas residents’ visits and spending. Also includes data on nights, purpose, region of UK visited and mode of travel. Breakdowns by nationality and area of residence are covered. The Quarter 4 (Oct to Dec) versions of this dataset up to 2023 are on a different webpage under the name "Overseas travel and tourism, quarterly". 
*   ### [Travel trends estimates: UK residents' visits abroad](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/leisureandtourism/datasets/ukresidentsvisitsabroad)

Annual estimates of visits and spending by UK residents abroad. Also includes data on nights, purpose, main country visited and mode of travel. Breakdowns by length of stay and nationality are covered. In 2019, new methods were introduced for this dataset. The 2009 to 2019 edition supersedes all previous time series editions of this dataset. We advise against using all editions listed before the 2019 edition. 
*   ### [Travel trends estimates: overseas residents in the UK](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/leisureandtourism/datasets/overseasresidentsvisitstotheuk)

Annual estimates of overseas residents’ visits and spending. Also includes data on nights, purpose, region of UK visited and mode of travel. Breakdowns by nationality and area of residence are covered. In 2019, new methods were introduced for this dataset. The 2009 to 2019 edition supersedes all previous time series editions of this dataset. We advise against using all editions listed before the 2019 edition. 
*   ### [Travelpac: travel to and from the UK](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/leisureandtourism/datasets/travelpac)

Estimates of international visits with details on traveller age and sex, trip purpose, length, and spending. From the International Passenger Survey (IPS).

Tourism: Supporting Key Government
Policies

With the UK poised to leave the European Union this year,
there is a very real need for the Government to support
sectors of the economy that are well positioned to provide
the country with economic growth and create employment
opportunities in the post-Brexit environment.
Tourism is one of the main sectors of the economy that is well placed to achieve
this. The UK continues to be not just one of the most popular destinations in the
world for visitors, but the World Economic Forum continues to rank the UK’s
tourism industry and infrastructure as one of the most competitive in the world.
We are therefore delighted that a Tourism Sector Deal has been agreed under the
Government’s Industrial Strategy. This is only the 10th sector deal to be announced
and highlights the Government’s increasing recognition of the economic importance
of the tourism industry and the opportunities and benefits that it can provide for the
UK economy and in supporting Government policy.
Two very important examples are regional development and soft power.
Regional Development
One of the main challenges for Government is to boost growth outside London and
the South East so as to address both the “North/South” divide and to support the
economies of rural and seaside communities which have lagged behind urban areas
in recovering from the Global Economic Crisis 10 years ago.
Tourism is one of the few industries that can directly support this objective quickly
and without substantial investment in new infrastructure. Despite the growth in city-
breaks, domestic tourism in the UK is largely composed of people in urban areas
travelling to rural and seaside destinations. The £25bn that these visitors spend
on breaks and holidays represents the single largest non-governmental transfer of
wealth to the economies of rural and seaside communities, creating 460,000 fulltime
jobs in these areas.
Soft Power
With the UK leaving the EU, one of the Government’s key objectives is to increase
the UK’s global influence. Tourism is one of the key means of achieving this. Studies
continue to show that enhancing and promoting a country’s cultural and education
offering in overseas markets is a key means of gaining greater global influence.
There strong linkages between the UK’s culture, education and tourism sectors.
Not only is heritage and culture the primary reason that people travel to the UK,
recent research by Universities UK shows that 88% of people who visit the UK for
educational purposes plan to return to the country as tourists  due to the strong
affinity that they build with the country as a result of gaining a qualification.
While the Sector Deal is a significant step forward, it is very much a first step.
There is much more that can be done to boost tourism growth post Brexit. This
publication therefore provides the data to support a range of policies, from tax and
visa reform to resolving structural issues in domestic tourism funding and delivery,
that need to be addressed if we are to maximise tourism growth.

Kate Nicholls

Tourism: Supporting Key Government
Policies

With the UK poised to leave the European Union this year,
there is a very real need for the Government to support
sectors of the economy that are well positioned to provide
the country with economic growth and create employment
opportunities in the post-Brexit environment.
Tourism is one of the main sectors of the economy that is well placed to achieve
this. The UK continues to be not just one of the most popular destinations in the
world for visitors, but the World Economic Forum continues to rank the UK’s
tourism industry and infrastructure as one of the most competitive in the world.
We are therefore delighted that a Tourism Sector Deal has been agreed under the
Government’s Industrial Strategy. This is only the 10th sector deal to be announced
and highlights the Government’s increasing recognition of the economic importance
of the tourism industry and the opportunities and benefits that it can provide for the
UK economy and in supporting Government policy.
Two very important examples are regional development and soft power.
Regional Development
One of the main challenges for Government is to boost growth outside London and
the South East so as to address both the “North/South” divide and to support the
economies of rural and seaside communities which have lagged behind urban areas
in recovering from the Global Economic Crisis 10 years ago.
Tourism is one of the few industries that can directly support this objective quickly
and without substantial investment in new infrastructure. Despite the growth in city-
breaks, domestic tourism in the UK is largely composed of people in urban areas
travelling to rural and seaside destinations. The £25bn that these visitors spend
on breaks and holidays represents the single largest non-governmental transfer of
wealth to the economies of rural and seaside communities, creating 460,000 fulltime
jobs in these areas.
Soft Power
With the UK leaving the EU, one of the Government’s key objectives is to increase
the UK’s global influence. Tourism is one of the key means of achieving this. Studies
continue to show that enhancing and promoting a country’s cultural and education
offering in overseas markets is a key means of gaining greater global influence.
There strong linkages between the UK’s culture, education and tourism sectors.
Not only is heritage and culture the primary reason that people travel to the UK,
recent research by Universities UK shows that 88% of people who visit the UK for
educational purposes plan to return to the country as tourists  due to the strong
affinity that they build with the country as a result of gaining a qualification.
While the Sector Deal is a significant step forward, it is very much a first step.
There is much more that can be done to boost tourism growth post Brexit. This
publication therefore provides the data to support a range of policies, from tax and
visa reform to resolving structural issues in domestic tourism funding and delivery,
that need to be addressed if we are to maximise tourism growth.

Kate Nicholls
Chair
