# Travel and tourism in the United Kingdom - statistics & facts

 Region  United Kingdom  United Kingdom 

 Choose a region: ![Image 1: United Kingdom](https://cdn.statcdn.com/static/icons/flag/iso/svg_flags/GB.svg) United Kingdom 

*   Overview
*   Editor’s Picks
*   Statistics

Many would agree that the United Kingdom might not have the most attractive climate for vacationers. What it does not lack in, however, is iconic touristic destinations. From Stonehenge, through the historic bustling streets of London and Edinburgh, to the Jurassic Coast, tourists are spoilt for choice. Travel and tourism is a vital part of the UK's economy, with the [total contribution of the industry to the UK's GDP](https://www.statista.com/statistics/598093/travel-and-tourism-gdp-total-contribution-united-kingdom-uk/) amounting to roughly 286 billion British pounds in 2024. While the sector's GDP footprint has surpassed pre-pandemic levels, the [contribution of travel and tourism to the UK's job market](https://www.statista.com/statistics/598098/travel-and-tourism-employment-contribution-united-kingdom-uk/) remained about two percent below 2019 figures that year.

  

## A rebound in overseas arrivals and record-breaking spending

Despite some metrics still trailing 2019 levels, the UK's travel and tourism industry has shown clear signs of recovery. In 2024, [inbound tourist visits in the UK](https://www.statista.com/statistics/287133/annual-number-of-overseas-visits-to-the-united-kingdom-uk/) grew by around three percent over the previous year, reaching approximately 39 million. With the rise in international travelers came a boost in revenue, as [international visitor expenditure](https://www.statista.com/statistics/287526/international-tourism-expenditure-in-the-united-kingdom-uk/) reached nearly 32 billion British pounds that year. The expenditure of travelers from the United States, the [leading inbound tourism market in the UK](https://www.statista.com/statistics/426417/leading-source-travel-markets-for-the-uk/) based on travel spending, topped seven billion British pounds in 2024, roughly 74 percent more than in 2019.

## Record outbound trips

Moving in the opposite direction, the [number of outbound tourist visits from the UK](https://www.statista.com/statistics/290516/total-annual-visits-abroad-by-united-kingdom-uk-residents/) reached 94.61 million in 2024, surpassing the pre-pandemic high for the first time. That year, the [leading countries visited by residents in the UK](https://www.statista.com/statistics/578815/most-visited-countries-united-kingdom-uk-residents/) was Spain, which recorded over 17 million visits; this was nearly double the second most visited destination, which was France. Meanwhile, when looking at the leading outbound travel markets in the UK based on the [growth in travel demand on Google](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1292404/uk-top-outbound-markets-by-google-travel-demand-growth/) as of January 2025, the United States, Spain, and Italy took the top three spots.

## Budget-minded travelers in a cost-squeezed economy

Among the Britons who decided to spend their holidays at home, over 87 billion British pounds were[spent on domestic tourism in Great Britain](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1255947/coronavirus-impact-domestic-travel-spending-britain/) in 2024.Looking at the [attitudes towards traveling in the UK](https://www.statista.com/forecasts/997936/attitudes-towards-traveling-in-the-uk/), a 2025 survey found that 35 percent of respondents always looked for the cheapest offers when planning a trip. With household budgets under continued pressure, the UK's weather and rising cost of living were tied as the [main barriers to overnight domestic trips in the UK](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1283970/main-barriers-to-overnight-domestic-trips-uk/), an April 2026 poll revealed, suggesting affordable options will remain a priority for British travelers.

# Tourist numbers to the UK down while global figures continue to rise

This article is more than 7 years old

A decrease in visitors coming to Britain and a fall in spending are in stark contrast to a worldwide increase in international arrivals, according to UN data

[Antonia Wilson](https://www.theguardian.com/profile/antonia-wilson)

Tue 22 Jan 2019 13.00 EST Last modified on Tue 22 Jan 2019 13.02 EST

Share

[Prefer the Guardian on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=theguardian.com)

The number of people visiting the UK on holiday fell in 2018. This was contrary to predictions and bucked the global travel trend, which saw worldwide international arrivals increase 6% year on year. The figure for worldwide arrivals has reached 1.4 bn, two years earlier than expected, according to the United Nations World Tourism Organization ([UNWTO](http://www2.unwto.org/)). In contrast, the UK saw a decline of 5.3% in overseas tourists and a 2.3% fall in spending, despite [earlier suggestions](https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2017/dec/26/uk-braced-for-record-number-of-tourists-in-2018)that a record year in 2017 would continue into 2018.

The drop in inbound tourism to the UK has been attributed to a fall in interest among Europeans, who account for two-thirds of overseas visitors. Research by VisitBritain showed that interest in visiting the UK since the Brexit referendum fell from 76% in August 2016 to 69% in autumn 2018.

Patricia Yates, a director at VisitBritain, predicted that visitors from Europe will continue to fall in 2019. In response, the organisation is launching a campaign called Friends of Europe, aimed at reassuring Europeans that they will receive a warm welcome and that Britain represents good value. Yates said that, despite the fall in the value of the pound, the UK is still seen as an expensive destination. Combined with uncertainty around Brexit, it means forward bookings are “very difficult”.

Globally, tourist arrival figures were highest in the Middle East (up 10%), Africa (up 7%), Asia and the Pacific, and Europe (both up 6%). The Americas were below the world average (up 3%), with Central America and the Caribbean seeing a fall of 2%, reflecting the impact of hurricanes Irma and Maria in late 2017, according to UNWTO. Growth has been driven by stable fuel prices, improved air links between destinations and strong outbound travel from emerging markets including Russia and the Middle East and some smaller Asian and Arab countries.

Outbound travel by UK residents saw growth in spending, up 4%, with an increase in travel to non-eurozone countries, such as Egypt and Turkey.

Looking ahead, the UNWTO said 2019 global arrivals are likely to drop back to 3%-4%, in line with historic growth trends, as global economic slowdown, uncertainty around Brexit, and geopolitical and trade tensions cause a “wait and see” attitude among investors and travellers.

The global figure is based on data reported by destinations around the world and measures arrivals that include an overnight stay. With an increase of 6% in tourist arrivals around the world, 2018 was the second-best year since 2010, following a strong 2017, which saw a rise of 7%.

“The growth of tourism in recent years confirms that the sector is today one of the most powerful drivers of economic growth and development. It is our responsibility to manage it in a sustainable manner and translate this expansion into real benefits for all countries and, particularly, to all local communities, creating opportunities for jobs and entrepreneurship and leaving no one behind,” said UNWTO secretary-general Zurab Pololikashvili.

# Tourist numbers to the UK down while global figures continue to rise

This article is more than 7 years old

A decrease in visitors coming to Britain and a fall in spending are in stark contrast to a worldwide increase in international arrivals, according to UN data

[Antonia Wilson](https://www.theguardian.com/profile/antonia-wilson)

Tue 22 Jan 2019 13.00 EST Last modified on Tue 22 Jan 2019 13.02 EST

Share

[Prefer the Guardian on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=theguardian.com)

The number of people visiting the UK on holiday fell in 2018. This was contrary to predictions and bucked the global travel trend, which saw worldwide international arrivals increase 6% year on year. The figure for worldwide arrivals has reached 1.4 bn, two years earlier than expected, according to the United Nations World Tourism Organization ([UNWTO](http://www2.unwto.org/)). In contrast, the UK saw a decline of 5.3% in overseas tourists and a 2.3% fall in spending, despite [earlier suggestions](https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2017/dec/26/uk-braced-for-record-number-of-tourists-in-2018)that a record year in 2017 would continue into 2018.

The drop in inbound tourism to the UK has been attributed to a fall in interest among Europeans, who account for two-thirds of overseas visitors. Research by VisitBritain showed that interest in visiting the UK since the Brexit referendum fell from 76% in August 2016 to 69% in autumn 2018.

Patricia Yates, a director at VisitBritain, predicted that visitors from Europe will continue to fall in 2019. In response, the organisation is launching a campaign called Friends of Europe, aimed at reassuring Europeans that they will receive a warm welcome and that Britain represents good value. Yates said that, despite the fall in the value of the pound, the UK is still seen as an expensive destination. Combined with uncertainty around Brexit, it means forward bookings are “very difficult”.

Globally, tourist arrival figures were highest in the Middle East (up 10%), Africa (up 7%), Asia and the Pacific, and Europe (both up 6%). The Americas were below the world average (up 3%), with Central America and the Caribbean seeing a fall of 2%, reflecting the impact of hurricanes Irma and Maria in late 2017, according to UNWTO. Growth has been driven by stable fuel prices, improved air links between destinations and strong outbound travel from emerging markets including Russia and the Middle East and some smaller Asian and Arab countries.

Outbound travel by UK residents saw growth in spending, up 4%, with an increase in travel to non-eurozone countries, such as Egypt and Turkey.

Looking ahead, the UNWTO said 2019 global arrivals are likely to drop back to 3%-4%, in line with historic growth trends, as global economic slowdown, uncertainty around Brexit, and geopolitical and trade tensions cause a “wait and see” attitude among investors and travellers.

The global figure is based on data reported by destinations around the world and measures arrivals that include an overnight stay. With an increase of 6% in tourist arrivals around the world, 2018 was the second-best year since 2010, following a strong 2017, which saw a rise of 7%.

“The growth of tourism in recent years confirms that the sector is today one of the most powerful drivers of economic growth and development. It is our responsibility to manage it in a sustainable manner and translate this expansion into real benefits for all countries and, particularly, to all local communities, creating opportunities for jobs and entrepreneurship and leaving no one behind,” said UNWTO secretary-general Zurab Pololikashvili.

# Tourism

By [Bastian Herre](https://ourworldindata.org/team/bastian-herre) and [Veronika Samborska](https://ourworldindata.org/team/veronika-samborska)

Cite this workReuse this work

*   Introduction
*   Charts

Tourism has massively increased in recent decades. Aviation has opened up travel from domestic to international. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of international visits had more than doubled since 2000.

Tourism can be important for both the travelers and the people in the countries they visit.

For visitors, traveling can increase their understanding of and appreciation for people in other countries and their cultures.

And in many countries, many people rely on tourism for their income. In some, it is one of the largest industries.

But tourism also has externalities: it [contributes](https://ourworldindata.org/co2-emissions-from-aviation) to global carbon emissions and can encroach on local environments and cultures.

On this page, you can find data and visualizations on the history and current state of tourism across the world.

# Tourism

By [Bastian Herre](https://ourworldindata.org/team/bastian-herre) and [Veronika Samborska](https://ourworldindata.org/team/veronika-samborska)

Cite this workReuse this work

*   Introduction
*   Charts

Tourism has massively increased in recent decades. Aviation has opened up travel from domestic to international. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of international visits had more than doubled since 2000.

Tourism can be important for both the travelers and the people in the countries they visit.

For visitors, traveling can increase their understanding of and appreciation for people in other countries and their cultures.

And in many countries, many people rely on tourism for their income. In some, it is one of the largest industries.

But tourism also has externalities: it [contributes](https://ourworldindata.org/co2-emissions-from-aviation) to global carbon emissions and can encroach on local environments and cultures.

On this page, you can find data and visualizations on the history and current state of tourism across the world.

A tourist stall selling various London and [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") related souvenirs on the edge of [Trafalgar Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trafalgar_Square "Trafalgar Square") on the [Strand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strand,_London "Strand, London")

Tourism in the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") is a major industry and contributor to the [UK economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_the_United_Kingdom "Economy of the United Kingdom"), which is the world's [ninth biggest tourist destination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Tourism_rankings "World Tourism rankings"), with over 40.1 million visiting in 2019, contributing a total of £234 billion to the GDP.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-2)

£23.1 billion was spent in the UK by foreign tourists in 2017. [VisitBritain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VisitBritain "VisitBritain") data shows that the United States remains the most valuable inbound market, with American visitors spending £2.1 billion in 2010.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-3) Nevertheless, the number of travellers originating from Europe is much larger than those travelling from North America: 21.5 million compared to 3.5 million American/Canadian visitors.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-4)

The country's principal tourist destinations are [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh"), [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford "Oxford"), [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge "Cambridge"), [York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York "York"), and [Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury "Canterbury"). The United Kingdom [hosts a total of 33 World Heritage sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_the_United_Kingdom "List of World Heritage Sites in the United Kingdom"), the 8th most in the world.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-5) The [Lonely Planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonely_Planet "Lonely Planet") travel guide voted [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") number 2, after [Bhutan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhutan "Bhutan"), as one of the best countries to visit in 2020.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-6) Some of the most popular cities include [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh") and [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester") and notable attractions include the [Palace of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Westminster "Palace of Westminster"), the [London Eye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Eye "London Eye") and [Edinburgh Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh_Castle "Edinburgh Castle").

The World Heritage Sites of the United Kingdom: cultural sites marked red, natural sites marked green, mixed site ([St Kilda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Kilda,_Scotland "St Kilda, Scotland")) marked blue. Names are abridged to fit on the map. [Greater London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_London "Greater London") is home to the cultural sites of [Maritime Greenwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich "Greenwich"), [Royal Botanical Gardens, Kew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Botanical_Gardens,_Kew "Royal Botanical Gardens, Kew"), [Tower of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_London "Tower of London"), and [Palace of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Westminster "Palace of Westminster") and [Westminster Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey") including [Saint Margaret's Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Margaret's,_Westminster "St Margaret's, Westminster").

Tourism first began to increase during the 17th century when wealthy Europeans would follow the ‘[Grand Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Tour "Grand Tour")’ of Western Europe which traditionally started in the United Kingdom before travelling to [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-7) Throughout the [Industrial Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution"), tourism continued to spike as people began to have more disposable income and technological advancements made transport more convenient and affordable. In 1841, [Thomas Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Cook "Thomas Cook"), founder of [Thomas Cook & Son](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Cook_&_Son "Thomas Cook & Son"), took 500 passengers by train on a return trip from [Leicester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leicester "Leicester") to [Loughborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loughborough "Loughborough").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:0-8) This was his first excursion and is seen as a significant milestone in the creation of the British tourism industry.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:0-8)

The world wars dampened the growth of the tourism sector, although after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") the government began putting measures in place to increase tourism, recognising its political and economic influence.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:1-9) By 1987, the [World Tourism Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Tourism_Organization "World Tourism Organization") estimated 3.4% of the UK's GDP came from tourism.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:1-9) More recently, budget airlines and cheap accommodation has caused almost continuous year-on-year growth. In more recent times, terrorist attacks in the UK such as the [7/7 bombings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7_July_2005_London_bombings "7 July 2005 London bombings") in 2005 have an expected negative impact on the tourism industry.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis") led to three consecutive years of the number of visitors from overseas decreasing for the only period between 2002 and 2017.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-10)

The United Kingdom is the 10th most visited country in the world and the 6th most visited country in Europe.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-11)

The [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom "COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom") affected tourism in the United Kingdom. In March 2020, the government decided to impose restrictions on all non-essential travel (both domestic and international). It was reported that in the month of April [Heathrow Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport "Heathrow Airport") was expecting 6.7 million passengers, but only 200,000 arrived which is roughly equivalent to a normal day.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-12) In April 2020, professional services firm [PricewaterhouseCoopers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PricewaterhouseCoopers "PricewaterhouseCoopers") expected that the worst affected sectors in the U.K. such as transport, hotels and food service could drop by at a minimum 15% or in the worst-case scenario by 40%.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-13)

The restrictions and lockdowns necessitated by the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom "COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom") (starting in March or April 2020) affected all sectors of the economy and "Tourism and hospitality suffered notable losses from the pandemic", according to March 2021 report published by the [Fraser of Allander Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraser_of_Allander_Institute "Fraser of Allander Institute"). The group provided detailed specifics for both domestic and international visits.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-14) COVID-19 lockdowns necessitated significantly reduced the number of visitors in 2020, and into 2021. Although the government announced a £56m "welcome back fund" in March 2021 to help councils and businesses in coastal towns prepare to welcome tourists back safely in summer, "as soon as the [roadmap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom#February_2021:_Variants_of_concern_and_vaccination_efficacy "COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom") allows" despite the [COVID-19 Alpha variant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SARS-CoV-2_Alpha_variant "SARS-CoV-2 Alpha variant") emerged.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-15)As of March 2021[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit), a 10-day quarantine period applies to people entering the UK from a number of "red list" countries.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-16)

As the country surpassed 100,000 COVID-19 related deaths, a [VisitBritain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VisitBritain "VisitBritain") report in January 2021 discussed the effects of the pandemic on domestic tourism within the UK in 2020, citing a significant reduction in spending, for an estimated decline of 62% over the previous year. The forecast for 2021 suggested that spending would increase by 79% over the previous year and that "the value of spending will be back to 84% of 2019 levels" by the end of 2021. The forecasts were based on predictions about the easing of travel restrictions and an increase in consumer confidence.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-17)

The same VisitBritain report provided the following estimate for "inbound tourism" in 2020: a "decline of 76% in visits to 9.7 million and a decline of 80% in spending to £5.7 billion". The forecast for 2021 indicated an estimated "11.7 million visits, up 21% on 2020, but only 29% of the 2019 level". Some £6.6 billion would be spent by inbound tourists, "up 16% on 2020 but only 23% of the 2019 level". An increase in the number of visits was expected as 2021 developed, but that would start slowly and tourism was not expected to come "even close to normal levels" during the year.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-18)

On 5 April 2021, [BBC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_News "BBC News") published an update on domestic tourism, indicating that travel restrictions were expected to be loosened during that month, at least for travel within England, Scotland and Wales. No announcement had been made as of early April by Northern Ireland.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-19) The tourism authority also indicated that there was a plan for the UK to loosen restrictions on international travel on 17 May, both inbound and outbound, but it was premature to predict whether those changes would actually commence at the expected time.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-20)

On 6 April 2021, [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN") published an update as to the tourism situation, particularly for readers in nations. Any visitors from "red list" countries were still not allowed to enter unless they were UK residents. "There's still not much to do in the UK right now ... although this lockdown is now being eased some restrictions will likely be in place until the summer", the report predicted, with June being the most likely time for tourism from other countries to begin a rebound.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-21)

It was possible that loosening of the UK's restrictions on inbound tourists would not commence as early as planned because sources in the European Union stated on 8 April 2021 that a "third wave of the pandemic [was sweeping] the continent". (Two days earlier, PM [Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson") had made it clear that "We don't want to see the virus being reimported into this country from abroad".)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-22) Of particular concern was the [B.1.1.7. variant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lineage_B.1.1.7 "Lineage B.1.1.7"), a mutation of the virus, "which [was] spreading rapidly in at least 27 and other European countries".[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-23)

Some restrictions on hospitality and domestic tourism were loosened in England on 12 April 2021; pubs and restaurants were allowed to open their outdoor facilities; non-essential stores opened; families were allowed to travel within England "in self-contained accommodation" and travel between Wales and England was fully permitted. Restrictions regarding tourism were not lifted in Scotland and Northern Ireland; in addition to permitting travel to and from England, Wales permitted non-essential retail stores to open.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-24)

In April 2022 same day as [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Ireland "Republic of Ireland"), [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland"), [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia"), [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore"), and other countries, COVID-19 tourism impact in the U.K. was officially ended by early April 2022 as the country ahead of [endemic phase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endemic_phase_of_COVID-19 "Endemic phase of COVID-19").

## Politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Politics")]

The [Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for Arts, Heritage and Tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Under_Secretary_of_State_for_Arts,_Heritage_and_Tourism "Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for Arts, Heritage and Tourism") is the [minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_(government) "Minister (government)") with responsibility over [tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism "Tourism") in England.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-25)

## Domestic tourism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Domestic tourism")]

Domestic tourism remains the biggest component of tourist spending in the UK, with 2008 expenditures totalling £21.9 billion, according to VisitBritain.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-VB2009-26) The national statistical agency also estimates that there were 126 million trips made in 2009.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-VB2009-26) The busiest period for domestic travel in the UK is during bank holidays and the summer months, with August being the busiest.

Visa requirements are different depending on the origin of the individual wishing to enter the United Kingdom.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:3-30) Some individuals are entitled to enter the United Kingdom without a visa and have no restrictions on their length of stay, work policies or study policies. These groups are: [British nationals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_nationality_law "British nationality law"), citizens of [Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations") countries who have the [right of abode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_of_abode_(United_Kingdom) "Right of abode (United Kingdom)"), [Irish citizens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_nationality_law "Irish nationality law") and until at least 31 December 2020, [European Union citizens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizenship_of_the_European_Union "Citizenship of the European Union") and citizens of [EFTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Free_Trade_Association "European Free Trade Association") member states.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:3-30) There are 56 other countries and territories that can stay in the UK for up to 6 months. Nationals of other countries are required to hold a Standard Visitor visa, costing £95, to be able to visit for up to 6 months.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-31)

[London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") is the most visited city in the United Kingdom, and some of the smaller town and cities attract a significant number of tourists.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-32) The country's other large cities such as [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh"), [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester") and [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool "Liverpool") draw large numbers, and some smaller cities have major [tourist attraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourist_attraction "Tourist attraction") landmarks.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-33) The university cities of [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford "Oxford") and [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge "Cambridge") are, despite their smaller population, recognised worldwide because of the [Oxbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxbridge "Oxbridge") universities’ legacies.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-34)

[VisitBritain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VisitBritain "VisitBritain"), the tourist board of Great Britain, analyses data from the [Office for National Statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_for_National_Statistics_(United_Kingdom) "Office for National Statistics (United Kingdom)") to estimate the number of visitors that attend each attraction.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:7-35) This can be difficult to measure for landmarks such as [Buckingham Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckingham_Palace "Buckingham Palace") or the [Palace of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Westminster "Palace of Westminster"), as many tourists visit the surrounding area without actually being admitted into the venue.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:7-35)

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Transport")]

Main article: [Transport in the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_in_the_United_Kingdom "Transport in the United Kingdom")

### Arriving in the United Kingdom

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Arriving in the United Kingdom")]

The United Kingdom only has one land border where Northern Ireland meets the Republic of Ireland.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-36) This border is considered an [open border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_border "Open border") due to the [Common Travel Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Travel_Area "Common Travel Area") arrangement and as a result is subject to minimal controls.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-37) The lack of control at the border makes it difficult to estimate the number of visitors from the [Republic of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Ireland "Republic of Ireland") into [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland "Northern Ireland").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-38) In 2018, the total number of international visits to the United Kingdom was 37.9 million.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-39) Out of the 37.9 million visitors, 29.06 million arrived by aeroplane, 4.81 million by boat and 4.04 million crossed from France using the [Channel Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_Tunnel "Channel Tunnel").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-40)

### Travelling within the United Kingdom

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Travelling within the United Kingdom")]

[![Image 42](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/DerryLondonderryStation.jpg/250px-DerryLondonderryStation.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DerryLondonderryStation.jpg)

[Derry~Londonderry railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derry_~_Londonderry_railway_station "Derry ~ Londonderry railway station") on the scenic [Belfast-Derry railway line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belfast-Derry_railway_line "Belfast-Derry railway line") run by [Northern Ireland Railways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Railways "Northern Ireland Railways")

With 48% of tourists using intracity buses, tubes, trams and metro trains; they are by far the most popular methods of transport.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:4-41) The next most common methods of transports are taxis and trains (outside town/city) with 27% and 23% respectively.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:4-41) Trains are used to travel between cities significantly more than aeroplanes, with only 1% of international visitors flying domestically.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:4-41) This has been attributed to the United Kingdom's vast rail network being the most economical way to travel.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-42) Despite [Uber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uber "Uber") being in a legal battle to operate in London, the rise of Uber and other [ride-sharing companies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridesharing_company "Ridesharing company") throughout the United Kingdom has led to them being used by 9% of international tourists and they are expected to further increase, reducing the market share of other methods of transport.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-43)

## Events, festivals and exhibitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Events, festivals and exhibitions")]

The United Kingdom plays host to a variety of events that attract both international and domestic tourists.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-44) Some of the United Kingdom's most famous festivals include [Notting Hill Carnival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notting_Hill_Carnival "Notting Hill Carnival"), [Glastonbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glastonbury "Glastonbury") and the [Edinburgh Fringe Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh_Festival_Fringe "Edinburgh Festival Fringe").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-45) These festivals not only hold cultural significance but are also a major economic component of the United Kingdom's tourist industry, with [Glastonbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glastonbury "Glastonbury") alone contributing £100 million to the economy annually.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-46) The beauty, real estate and arms industries are some of the many industries that hold trade shows and exhibitions year-round throughout the United Kingdom, with the majority being held in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") or [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham "Birmingham"). [VisitBritain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VisitBritain "VisitBritain") has estimated in 2015 there were 65 million day visits centred around events, festivals and exhibitions and in total, they accounted for 5% of all tourist day visits and a net spend of £3.6 billion.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-47)

Launch of GREAT campaign, Australia

In 2011, [VisitBritain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VisitBritain "VisitBritain") launched GREAT, one of a £100 million marketing campaign, promoting the United Kingdom through culture, heritage, sport, music, countryside, food and shopping.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-48) The campaign has successfully reached over 145 countries and united both the public and private sectors to generate growth and jobs.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-49) Overall, inbound and domestic marketing have generated £1 billion in additional visitor spend, of which, £800 million can be attributed to the GREAT campaign.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-50)

## Shopping

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Shopping")]

[![Image 44](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Harrods_at_night.jpg/250px-Harrods_at_night.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harrods_at_night.jpg)

Harrods at night

Shopping is one of the most common activities for overseas visitors to the United Kingdom with 58% of all visits and 70% of leisure visits involving shopping.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-51) Each year, roughly 277,000 people travel to the United Kingdom for the primary reason of personal shopping.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:5-52) The total spend of these visits is around £168 million.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:5-52) The most commonly purchased items are clothes and shoes with just over 40% of visitors purchasing at least one item of clothing or a pair of shoes.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:5-52)

Ornamental souvenirs representing items found in the United Kingdom such as post office boxes, [black cabs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hackney_carriage#Black_cabs "Hackney carriage") and London buses are commonly found in souvenir shops over the United Kingdom.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-53) Other examples of commonly purchased souvenirs include: [Union Jack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Jack "Union Jack") branded goods, items from famous department stores like [Harrods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrods "Harrods") and [Selfridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selfridges "Selfridges") and memorabilia surrounding the [British royal family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_royal_family "British royal family").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-54)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Tourist_Stall%2C_Trafalgar_Square%2C_London_-_May_2009.jpg/250px-Tourist_Stall%2C_Trafalgar_Square%2C_London_-_May_2009.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tourist_Stall,_Trafalgar_Square,_London_-_May_2009.jpg)

A tourist stall selling various London and [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") related souvenirs on the edge of [Trafalgar Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trafalgar_Square "Trafalgar Square") on the [Strand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strand,_London "Strand, London")

Tourism in the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") is a major industry and contributor to the [UK economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_the_United_Kingdom "Economy of the United Kingdom"), which is the world's [ninth biggest tourist destination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Tourism_rankings "World Tourism rankings"), with over 40.1 million visiting in 2019, contributing a total of £234 billion to the GDP.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-2)

£23.1 billion was spent in the UK by foreign tourists in 2017. [VisitBritain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VisitBritain "VisitBritain") data shows that the United States remains the most valuable inbound market, with American visitors spending £2.1 billion in 2010.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-3) Nevertheless, the number of travellers originating from Europe is much larger than those travelling from North America: 21.5 million compared to 3.5 million American/Canadian visitors.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-4)

The country's principal tourist destinations are [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh"), [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford "Oxford"), [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge "Cambridge"), [York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York "York"), and [Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury "Canterbury"). The United Kingdom [hosts a total of 33 World Heritage sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_the_United_Kingdom "List of World Heritage Sites in the United Kingdom"), the 8th most in the world.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-5) The [Lonely Planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonely_Planet "Lonely Planet") travel guide voted [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") number 2, after [Bhutan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhutan "Bhutan"), as one of the best countries to visit in 2020.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-6) Some of the most popular cities include [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh") and [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester") and notable attractions include the [Palace of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Westminster "Palace of Westminster"), the [London Eye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Eye "London Eye") and [Edinburgh Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh_Castle "Edinburgh Castle").

The World Heritage Sites of the United Kingdom: cultural sites marked red, natural sites marked green, mixed site ([St Kilda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Kilda,_Scotland "St Kilda, Scotland")) marked blue. Names are abridged to fit on the map. [Greater London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_London "Greater London") is home to the cultural sites of [Maritime Greenwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich "Greenwich"), [Royal Botanical Gardens, Kew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Botanical_Gardens,_Kew "Royal Botanical Gardens, Kew"), [Tower of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_London "Tower of London"), and [Palace of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Westminster "Palace of Westminster") and [Westminster Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey") including [Saint Margaret's Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Margaret's,_Westminster "St Margaret's, Westminster").

Tourism first began to increase during the 17th century when wealthy Europeans would follow the ‘[Grand Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Tour "Grand Tour")’ of Western Europe which traditionally started in the United Kingdom before travelling to [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-7) Throughout the [Industrial Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution"), tourism continued to spike as people began to have more disposable income and technological advancements made transport more convenient and affordable. In 1841, [Thomas Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Cook "Thomas Cook"), founder of [Thomas Cook & Son](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Cook_&_Son "Thomas Cook & Son"), took 500 passengers by train on a return trip from [Leicester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leicester "Leicester") to [Loughborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loughborough "Loughborough").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:0-8) This was his first excursion and is seen as a significant milestone in the creation of the British tourism industry.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:0-8)

The world wars dampened the growth of the tourism sector, although after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") the government began putting measures in place to increase tourism, recognising its political and economic influence.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:1-9) By 1987, the [World Tourism Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Tourism_Organization "World Tourism Organization") estimated 3.4% of the UK's GDP came from tourism.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:1-9) More recently, budget airlines and cheap accommodation has caused almost continuous year-on-year growth. In more recent times, terrorist attacks in the UK such as the [7/7 bombings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7_July_2005_London_bombings "7 July 2005 London bombings") in 2005 have an expected negative impact on the tourism industry.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis") led to three consecutive years of the number of visitors from overseas decreasing for the only period between 2002 and 2017.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-10)

The United Kingdom is the 10th most visited country in the world and the 6th most visited country in Europe.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-11)

The [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom "COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom") affected tourism in the United Kingdom. In March 2020, the government decided to impose restrictions on all non-essential travel (both domestic and international). It was reported that in the month of April [Heathrow Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport "Heathrow Airport") was expecting 6.7 million passengers, but only 200,000 arrived which is roughly equivalent to a normal day.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-12) In April 2020, professional services firm [PricewaterhouseCoopers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PricewaterhouseCoopers "PricewaterhouseCoopers") expected that the worst affected sectors in the U.K. such as transport, hotels and food service could drop by at a minimum 15% or in the worst-case scenario by 40%.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-13)

The restrictions and lockdowns necessitated by the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom "COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom") (starting in March or April 2020) affected all sectors of the economy and "Tourism and hospitality suffered notable losses from the pandemic", according to March 2021 report published by the [Fraser of Allander Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraser_of_Allander_Institute "Fraser of Allander Institute"). The group provided detailed specifics for both domestic and international visits.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-14) COVID-19 lockdowns necessitated significantly reduced the number of visitors in 2020, and into 2021. Although the government announced a £56m "welcome back fund" in March 2021 to help councils and businesses in coastal towns prepare to welcome tourists back safely in summer, "as soon as the [roadmap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom#February_2021:_Variants_of_concern_and_vaccination_efficacy "COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom") allows" despite the [COVID-19 Alpha variant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SARS-CoV-2_Alpha_variant "SARS-CoV-2 Alpha variant") emerged.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-15)As of March 2021[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit), a 10-day quarantine period applies to people entering the UK from a number of "red list" countries.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-16)

As the country surpassed 100,000 COVID-19 related deaths, a [VisitBritain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VisitBritain "VisitBritain") report in January 2021 discussed the effects of the pandemic on domestic tourism within the UK in 2020, citing a significant reduction in spending, for an estimated decline of 62% over the previous year. The forecast for 2021 suggested that spending would increase by 79% over the previous year and that "the value of spending will be back to 84% of 2019 levels" by the end of 2021. The forecasts were based on predictions about the easing of travel restrictions and an increase in consumer confidence.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-17)

The same VisitBritain report provided the following estimate for "inbound tourism" in 2020: a "decline of 76% in visits to 9.7 million and a decline of 80% in spending to £5.7 billion". The forecast for 2021 indicated an estimated "11.7 million visits, up 21% on 2020, but only 29% of the 2019 level". Some £6.6 billion would be spent by inbound tourists, "up 16% on 2020 but only 23% of the 2019 level". An increase in the number of visits was expected as 2021 developed, but that would start slowly and tourism was not expected to come "even close to normal levels" during the year.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-18)

On 5 April 2021, [BBC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_News "BBC News") published an update on domestic tourism, indicating that travel restrictions were expected to be loosened during that month, at least for travel within England, Scotland and Wales. No announcement had been made as of early April by Northern Ireland.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-19) The tourism authority also indicated that there was a plan for the UK to loosen restrictions on international travel on 17 May, both inbound and outbound, but it was premature to predict whether those changes would actually commence at the expected time.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-20)

On 6 April 2021, [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN") published an update as to the tourism situation, particularly for readers in nations. Any visitors from "red list" countries were still not allowed to enter unless they were UK residents. "There's still not much to do in the UK right now ... although this lockdown is now being eased some restrictions will likely be in place until the summer", the report predicted, with June being the most likely time for tourism from other countries to begin a rebound.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-21)

It was possible that loosening of the UK's restrictions on inbound tourists would not commence as early as planned because sources in the European Union stated on 8 April 2021 that a "third wave of the pandemic [was sweeping] the continent". (Two days earlier, PM [Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson") had made it clear that "We don't want to see the virus being reimported into this country from abroad".)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-22) Of particular concern was the [B.1.1.7. variant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lineage_B.1.1.7 "Lineage B.1.1.7"), a mutation of the virus, "which [was] spreading rapidly in at least 27 and other European countries".[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-23)

Some restrictions on hospitality and domestic tourism were loosened in England on 12 April 2021; pubs and restaurants were allowed to open their outdoor facilities; non-essential stores opened; families were allowed to travel within England "in self-contained accommodation" and travel between Wales and England was fully permitted. Restrictions regarding tourism were not lifted in Scotland and Northern Ireland; in addition to permitting travel to and from England, Wales permitted non-essential retail stores to open.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-24)

In April 2022 same day as [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Ireland "Republic of Ireland"), [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland"), [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia"), [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore"), and other countries, COVID-19 tourism impact in the U.K. was officially ended by early April 2022 as the country ahead of [endemic phase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endemic_phase_of_COVID-19 "Endemic phase of COVID-19").

## Politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Politics")]

The [Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for Arts, Heritage and Tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Under_Secretary_of_State_for_Arts,_Heritage_and_Tourism "Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for Arts, Heritage and Tourism") is the [minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_(government) "Minister (government)") with responsibility over [tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism "Tourism") in England.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-25)

## Domestic tourism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Domestic tourism")]

Domestic tourism remains the biggest component of tourist spending in the UK, with 2008 expenditures totalling £21.9 billion, according to VisitBritain.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-VB2009-26) The national statistical agency also estimates that there were 126 million trips made in 2009.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-VB2009-26) The busiest period for domestic travel in the UK is during bank holidays and the summer months, with August being the busiest.

Visa requirements are different depending on the origin of the individual wishing to enter the United Kingdom.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:3-30) Some individuals are entitled to enter the United Kingdom without a visa and have no restrictions on their length of stay, work policies or study policies. These groups are: [British nationals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_nationality_law "British nationality law"), citizens of [Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations") countries who have the [right of abode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_of_abode_(United_Kingdom) "Right of abode (United Kingdom)"), [Irish citizens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_nationality_law "Irish nationality law") and until at least 31 December 2020, [European Union citizens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizenship_of_the_European_Union "Citizenship of the European Union") and citizens of [EFTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Free_Trade_Association "European Free Trade Association") member states.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:3-30) There are 56 other countries and territories that can stay in the UK for up to 6 months. [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") is the most visited city in the United Kingdom, and some of the smaller town and cities attract a significant number of tourists.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-32) The country's other large cities such as [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh"), [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester") and [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool "Liverpool") draw large numbers, and some smaller cities have major [tourist attraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourist_attraction "Tourist attraction") landmarks.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-33) The university cities of [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford "Oxford") and [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge "Cambridge") are, despite their smaller population, recognised worldwide because of the [Oxbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxbridge "Oxbridge") universities’ legacies.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-34)

[VisitBritain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VisitBritain "VisitBritain"), the tourist board of Great Britain, analyses data from the [Office for National Statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_for_National_Statistics_(United_Kingdom) "Office for National Statistics (United Kingdom)") to estimate the number of visitors that attend each attraction.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:7-35) This can be difficult to measure for landmarks such as [Buckingham Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckingham_Palace "Buckingham Palace") or the [Palace of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Westminster "Palace of Westminster"), as many tourists visit the surrounding area without actually being admitted into the venue.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:7-35)

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Transport")]

Main article: [Transport in the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_in_the_United_Kingdom "Transport in the United Kingdom")

### Arriving in the United Kingdom

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Arriving in the United Kingdom")]

The United Kingdom only has one land border where Northern Ireland meets the Republic of Ireland.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-36) This border is considered an [open border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_border "Open border") due to the [Common Travel Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Travel_Area "Common Travel Area") arrangement and as a result is subject to minimal controls.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-37) The lack of control at the border makes it difficult to estimate the number of visitors from the [Republic of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Ireland "Republic of Ireland") into [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland "Northern Ireland").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-38) In 2018, the total number of international visits to the United Kingdom was 37.9 million.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-39) Out of the 37.9 million visitors, 29.06 million arrived by aeroplane, 4.81 million by boat and 4.04 million crossed from France using the [Channel Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_Tunnel "Channel Tunnel").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-40)

### Travelling within the United Kingdom

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Travelling within the United Kingdom")]

[![Image 42](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/DerryLondonderryStation.jpg/250px-DerryLondonderryStation.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DerryLondonderryStation.jpg)

[Derry~Londonderry railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derry_~_Londonderry_railway_station "Derry ~ Londonderry railway station") on the scenic [Belfast-Derry railway line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belfast-Derry_railway_line "Belfast-Derry railway line") run by [Northern Ireland Railways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Railways "Northern Ireland Railways")

With 48% of tourists using intracity buses, tubes, trams and metro trains; they are by far the most popular methods of transport.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:4-41) The next most common methods of transports are taxis and trains (outside town/city) with 27% and 23% respectively.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:4-41) Trains are used to travel between cities significantly more than aeroplanes, with only 1% of international visitors flying domestically.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:4-41) This has been attributed to the United Kingdom's vast rail network being the most economical way to travel.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-42) Despite [Uber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uber "Uber") being in a legal battle to operate in London, the rise of Uber and other [ride-sharing companies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridesharing_company "Ridesharing company") throughout the United Kingdom has led to them being used by 9% of international tourists and they are expected to further increase, reducing the market share of other methods of transport.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-43)

## Events, festivals and exhibitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Events, festivals and exhibitions")]

The United Kingdom plays host to a variety of events that attract both international and domestic tourists.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-44) Some of the United Kingdom's most famous festivals include [Notting Hill Carnival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notting_Hill_Carnival "Notting Hill Carnival"), [Glastonbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glastonbury "Glastonbury") and the [Edinburgh Fringe Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh_Festival_Fringe "Edinburgh Festival Fringe").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-45) These festivals not only hold cultural significance but are also a major economic component of the United Kingdom's tourist industry, with [Glastonbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glastonbury "Glastonbury") alone contributing £100 million to the economy annually.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-46) The beauty, real estate and arms industries are some of the many industries that hold trade shows and exhibitions year-round throughout the United Kingdom, with the majority being held in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") or [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham "Birmingham"). [VisitBritain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VisitBritain "VisitBritain") has estimated in 2015 there were 65 million day visits centred around events, festivals and exhibitions and in total, they accounted for 5% of all tourist day visits and a net spend of £3.6 billion.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-47)

In 2011, [VisitBritain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VisitBritain "VisitBritain") launched GREAT, one of a £100 million marketing campaign, promoting the United Kingdom through culture, heritage, sport, music, countryside, food and shopping.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-48) The campaign has successfully reached over 145 countries and united both the public and private sectors to generate growth and jobs.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-49) Overall, inbound and domestic marketing have generated £1 billion in additional visitor spend, of which, £800 million can be attributed to the GREAT campaign.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-50)

## Shopping

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Shopping")]

[![Image 44](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Harrods_at_night.jpg/250px-Harrods_at_night.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harrods_at_night.jpg)

Harrods at night

Shopping is one of the most common activities for overseas visitors to the United Kingdom with 58% of all visits and 70% of leisure visits involving shopping.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-51) Each year, roughly 277,000 people travel to the United Kingdom for the primary reason of personal shopping.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:5-52) The total spend of these visits is around £168 million.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:5-52) The most commonly purchased items are clothes and shoes with just over 40% of visitors purchasing at least one item of clothing or a pair of shoes.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:5-52)

Ornamental souvenirs representing items found in the United Kingdom such as post office boxes, [black cabs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hackney_carriage#Black_cabs "Hackney carriage") and London buses are commonly found in souvenir shops over the United Kingdom.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-53) Other examples of commonly purchased souvenirs include: [Union Jack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Jack "Union Jack") branded goods, items from famous department stores like [Harrods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrods "Harrods") and [Selfridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selfridges "Selfridges") and memorabilia surrounding the [British royal family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_royal_family "British royal family").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-54)

# Tourism

By [Bastian Herre](https://ourworldindata.org/team/bastian-herre) and [Veronika Samborska](https://ourworldindata.org/team/veronika-samborska)

Cite this workReuse this work

*   Introduction
*   Charts

Tourism has massively increased in recent decades. Aviation has opened up travel from domestic to international. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of international visits had more than doubled since 2000.

Tourism can be important for both the travelers and the people in the countries they visit.

For visitors, traveling can increase their understanding of and appreciation for people in other countries and their cultures.

And in many countries, many people rely on tourism for their income. In some, it is one of the largest industries.

But tourism also has externalities: it [contributes](https://ourworldindata.org/co2-emissions-from-aviation) to global carbon emissions and can encroach on local environments and cultures.

On this page, you can find data and visualizations on the history and current state of tourism across the world.

# Tourism

By [Bastian Herre](https://ourworldindata.org/team/bastian-herre) and [Veronika Samborska](https://ourworldindata.org/team/veronika-samborska)

Cite this workReuse this work

*   Introduction
*   Charts

Tourism has massively increased in recent decades. Aviation has opened up travel from domestic to international. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of international visits had more than doubled since 2000.

Tourism can be important for both the travelers and the people in the countries they visit.

For visitors, traveling can increase their understanding of and appreciation for people in other countries and their cultures.

And in many countries, many people rely on tourism for their income. In some, it is one of the largest industries.

But tourism also has externalities: it [contributes](https://ourworldindata.org/co2-emissions-from-aviation) to global carbon emissions and can encroach on local environments and cultures.

On this page, you can find data and visualizations on the history and current state of tourism across the world.

The Tourism Data Blackout: Why the World's Most-Cited Travel Statistics Stopped in 2019 # The Tourism Data Blackout: Why the World's Most-Cited Travel Statistics Stopped in 2019 ![Image 2: Amina Khalidi](https://evisas-production.lon1.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/blog/54013072-2de5-43ab-b4f8-829612390467.jpg)Amina Khalidi August 23, 2026 34 min read ![Image 3: The Tourism Data Blackout: Why the World's Most-Cited Travel Statistics Stopped in 2019](https://evisas-production.lon1.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/blog/e829a168-ccad-44a6-a85e-3331d4012cbd.png) The World Bank's figure for international tourist arrivals worldwide is 2,403,074,088. It is precise down to a single traveller. It is free, it has an open API, it is licensed for reuse, and it sits at the top of the search results for anyone who needs a tourism number in a hurry. It is also from 2019. We queried the World Bank's public data API on 18 August 2026, and every year from 2020 onward came back empty. International travel is one of the largest industries on earth and one of the most heavily reported. It is also measured by a set of shared datasets that have quietly fallen out of date, contradict each other in ways that are rarely acknowledged, revise themselves without announcement, and leave at least one enormous question with no authoritative answer at all. We audited the sources the industry runs on. Here is what is current, what is frozen, what it costs, what changes after you quote it, and what nobody is measuring. ## The headline finding **The World Bank's headline tourism indicators have not been updated past 2019.** It is not only arrivals. Its world figures for international tourism receipts, and for receipts as a share of total exports, stop in the same place. We queried all three series for every year from 2015 to 2024. All three return values through 2019 and nothing at all from 2020 onward. The series was never backfilled through the disruption of the early 2020s, and five years on the gap remains. ![Image 4: Chart 1. Source: World Bank Open Data, World Development Indicators, indicator ST.INT.ARVL, world aggregate. Queried via the public API and verified 18 August 2026. Values for 2020 to 2024 return empty.](https://evisas-production.lon1.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/landing-pages/assets/3745f7e9-2e40-44ce-9494-be068b320a13.png) **Chart 1.** Source: World Bank Open Data, World Development Indicators, indicator **ST.INT.ARVL**, world aggregate. Queried via the public API and verified 18 August 2026. Values for 2020 to 2024 return empty. That matters more than a technical footnote suggests, because World Bank data is the default source for anyone who needs a tourism number in a hurry. It is free, it has an open API, it is licensed for reuse, and it sits at the top of search results. It is also, for this particular family of indicators, showing you the world as it was seven years ago. Individual countries may carry more recent entries than the world aggregate does, so the finding is stated here for the world series specifically. That distinction matters, and it is the kind of distinction that gets lost the moment a figure is lifted out of its source and into a slide. ## How far behind each source is The World Bank is the extreme case, but it is not the only one. We measured the gap between the end of each source's latest published data period and today. ![Image 5: Chart 2. Source: eVisas.com analysis, August 2026. Lag measured from the end of each source's latest published data period. Analytical reports without a data period, such as the OECD's, are measured from publication.](https://evisas-production.lon1.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/landing-pages/assets/d70d3844-12b5-40b2-bdfd-1d2e92548acf.png) **Chart 2.** Source: [eVisas.com](http://evisas.com/) analysis, August 2026. Lag measured from the end of each source's latest published data period. Analytical reports without a data period, such as the OECD's, are measured from publication. Most of the field is in reasonable shape. Eight of the twelve sources we checked are between two and eight months behind, which for international statistics is close to as good as it gets. IATA publishes monthly and its [**June 2026 analysis**](https://www.iata.org/en/iata-repository/publications/economic-reports/air-passenger-market-analysis-june-2026) came out on 30 July 2026. UN Tourism, Eurostat and the UK Home Office are all five months behind. Then there is a cliff. ICAO's air transport statistics and UN DESA's migrant stock are twenty months behind. UN Tourism's Visa Openness Report, the closest thing the world has to an official measure of how hard it is to cross a border, is thirty two months behind. And the World Bank's tourism series is eighty months behind, which is to say six years and eight months. The ICAO case deserves a moment on its own, because it shows how a source can look current and not be. ICAO has published its Annual Report of the Council for 2025. What it has not published is the statistics that normally accompany it. The document that should contain the 2025 global passenger totals is a placeholder carrying a single line, in all six United Nations languages, saying that documentation will be posted as it becomes available. The most recent global passenger total ICAO has issued is for[**2024: 4,669 million passengers carried on scheduled services**](https://www.icao.int/about-icao/AnnualReport2024/world-air-transport-2024), a figure ICAO itself labels preliminary. ## What is actually current, and what it costs The problem is that the stale sources and the current ones look identical from the outside. So does the free data and the data that costs thousands.
